Identifies responsiveness/focus-visible/truncation/hydration as browser-only signals no unit/typecheck gate observes

evals.prompt: I'll have the QA sub-agent kick off the full gate suite in the background and end its turn waiting for it to finish, then read the result. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: No -- a backgrounded gate loses its verdict. A sub-agent's own background task does not reliably notify the parent once the sub-agent has exited, and the turn ends before the run completes, so the result lands in a buffer nobody reads. Run gate/verification commands in the FOREGROUND (blocking) so the verdict is in the agent's own report, OR redirect output to a file the parent explicitly reads AFTER the process ends (a machine-readable last-run status file works well). Never end a turn 'waiting' on a background task whose completion notifies only the exited turn. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Rejects backgrounding a verification run whose completion notifies only the exited sub-agent turn
Requires foreground/blocking execution or an explicit-read-after-exit file (e.g. a status file)
Explains the verdict is otherwise lost to a buffer nobody reads
Does not assume the parent auto-receives a sub-agent's background result

evals.prompt: The owner is firing off ten separate pieces of UI feedback in a row. I'm dispatching each to a background lane in parallel as they arrive and staying quiet to maximize throughput. Right call?
evals.expected_output: Dispatch in parallel, but don't stay silent -- silent throughput is indistinguishable from ignoring them and escalates frustration even while work is running. On each burst the FIRST action is to capture every item into a visible tracked list and reply with the ordered plan plus what is already in flight; dispatch second. One honest 'captured all ten, here's the order, these three are already running' beats silent parallelism. Acknowledge first, optimise throughput second. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Keeps parallel dispatch but requires an explicit acknowledgement/plan reply first
Captures every feedback item into a visible tracked list rather than only dispatching
Explains that silent throughput reads as not listening
Orders: acknowledge + plan first, dispatch second

evals.prompt: A subagent I dispatched just sent a task-'completed' notification, but it had armed a background monitor. There's remaining work, so I'll immediately dispatch a second lane into the same worktree to finish it. OK?
evals.expected_output: Confirm the subagent is actually IDLE first. A 'completed' notification is not proof of terminal completion: on a harness that fires 'completed' each time an agent stops with no live background children of its own (and can notify the same task-id more than once), a subagent that armed a background monitor/watch cycles stop->wake and emits 'completed' on each stop -- so a single 'completed' is one of several, not done. The tell: a repeated 'completed' for the same task-id, or the agent's own last report still saying 'waiting.' Check its live state and those tells before dispatching a duplicate into the SAME worktree, where a collision corrupts the run. This is the dispatcher mirror of 'a backgrounded gate loses its verdict' -- there the doer drops a result, here the watcher acts on a not-yet-final one. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Does not treat a 'completed' notification as proof the subagent is idle, especially with a background monitor armed
Requires confirming the agent's live idle state before dispatching a duplicate
Uses the tell -- a repeated 'completed' for the same task-id, or the agent's report still 'waiting' -- to detect a not-yet-final signal
Flags the same-worktree collision risk

evals.prompt: A background subagent's transcript file hasn't grown in four minutes. I'm going to treat the lane as hung, kill it, and re-dispatch the work. Reasonable?
evals.expected_output: No -- a transcript's size or mtime is not a liveness signal, and killing the lane is a destructive, shared-state action. A transcript can lag a working agent by many minutes (a long tool call, a quiet reasoning stretch, buffered/flushed-late output) and can look equally 'recent' for an agent that already exited -- so a stat-based 'hung' inference cuts both ways: it kills a still-working lane (losing its in-flight work and worktree state) or trusts a dead one. Judge liveness from the agent's ACTUAL product -- a fresh work-tree diff or new commit, a live child process, an owned port/PID, or a direct ping it answers -- not the transcript file's age. Confirm the agent is genuinely idle by a positive signal before terminating (principle 9 -- closing or deleting shared state needs evidence, not presumption). If nothing but the transcript is observable, the honest state is UNVERIFIED, not 'dead.' This is the inverse of the idle-before-duplicate case: a false-negative liveness read leading to a destructive kill, not a false-positive 'completed' leading to a duplicate dispatch. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Rejects transcript/output-file size or mtime as a liveness signal in either direction
Requires a positive liveness signal (work-tree diff, new commit, live process, owned port/PID, answered ping) before judging the lane
Treats killing a lane as a destructive shared-state action to confirm before, and labels a transcript-only state UNVERIFIED not dead
Distinguishes the destructive false-negative-kill error from the false-positive-completed duplicate-dispatch error

evals.prompt: Our dev server rewrites a tracked config file on boot, and a pre-commit gate asserts that file's exact contents, so every commit fails while the server runs. I keep stopping the server to commit. Better pattern?
evals.expected_output: Serve and commit from separate trees. A long-running process (dev server, codegen/asset watcher) that rewrites a tracked, gate-asserted file on boot keeps that file dirty for its whole lifetime, so every commit from the same working tree fails on a 'modified config' nobody edited -- the stop-server/restore/re-commit dance is the symptom. Give the running stack its own worktree/checkout so the commit tree stays clean; if one tree is unavoidable, make the process write to a gitignored/untracked path, or stop it and restore the file before committing. Where a legitimate tool rewrites the file, prefer a gate that asserts its shape/schema over its exact bytes. This is a single-tree serve-vs-commit deadlock -- distinct from 'never build against a directory a running server is serving' (a stale-asset ship failure) and from out-of-tree scratch crossing commit metadata between lanes. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Identifies the shared single tree as the root: a running process dirties a tracked, gate-asserted file so the commit gate fails
Recommends serving from a separate worktree/checkout from the one you commit from
Offers the one-tree fallbacks -- gitignore/untrack the rewritten path, or stop-and-restore before commit -- and prefers a schema/shape assertion over exact bytes
Distinguishes the serve-vs-commit deadlock from build-against-served-dir and from out-of-tree-scratch metadata crossing

evals.prompt: An agent is about to start on a feature. The repo's module-ownership map says its lane owns api/, and the GitHub issue for the feature is assigned to it. No draft PR exists, no worktree is open, and there are no commits yet. Is it clear to open a worktree and start building?
evals.expected_output: Not on that evidence alone. The ownership map is a write-lock, not a work-lock: 'this lane owns api/' says who may WRITE api/, not whether someone is already BUILDING this feature (possibly from other files, like web/ or a shared lib). And a forge assignment is intent, not progress -- an assigned issue with no draft PR, no worktree, and no commits is unclaimed in practice (assigned != in-progress). Before opening the worktree, check for an active lane on the OBJECTIVE (not just file ownership): running workers, open/draft PRs, git worktree list. Then announce-then-take -- claim the objective with a draft PR or a posted 'taking this' BEFORE opening the worktree, never after; take-then-announce races two lanes onto the same work. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Distinguishes the ownership map (write-lock on a file) from a work-lock on the objective
Treats the assignment as intent not progress (assigned != in-progress) given no draft PR/worktree/commits
Requires checking for an active lane on the objective before starting, not just file ownership
Requires announce-then-take: claim the objective before opening the worktree, not after

evals.prompt: I'm sizing a heavy write fan-out on a shared machine. My probe reads 84% free RAM -- comfortable -- so I'm about to spawn three more lanes. (Swap is ~76% consumed but I only glanced once; the session has felt slow and nothing has landed in a while.) Green light?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't spawn. Free-RAM percentage fails open under thrash: it is a post-mitigation number (the OS has already paged out, evicted caches, and compressed memory to relieve pressure), so it reads healthiest exactly when the machine is most degraded. 84% free with swap ~76% consumed and nothing landing is a machine already shedding load. Gate on the SWAP TREND, sampled at least twice seconds apart, on its computed DIRECTION not its level -- swap that is climbing stops the spawn even at high free RAM. Free RAM may corroborate a STOP but must never on its own authorize a SPAWN. And the other two signals here already say stop: the session is slow and nothing has landed -- an observed collapse in work rate IS the resource signal and outranks any green metric. Probe free disk, worktree count, and the live-lane count too (a fan-out sized against memory alone dies of disk), and re-probe before each spawn -- never compute a ceiling once and burst up to it. (fanout-host-sizing.md.)
expectations: Refuses the spawn despite 84% free RAM; names free-RAM% as a post-mitigation figure that fails open under thrash
Gates on the swap TREND sampled twice (direction, not level); free RAM may corroborate a stop but never authorize a spawn
Treats the slow session / nothing-landing as a work-rate-collapse resource signal that outranks the green metric
Adds free disk, worktree count, and live-lane count to the probe and re-probes before each spawn

evals.prompt: I have one implementation lane running a consolidated deliverable. The owner keeps sending new requirements -- this is the fifth 'also add X' in a couple hours. My instinct is to interrupt the lane and re-brief it each time so its scope stays current. It hasn't produced a branch or commit yet. Right approach?
evals.expected_output: No -- interrupt-and-re-brief is why it has shipped nothing. Each interrupt lands mid-orient and that partial state isn't resumable, so the lane restarts its orientation every time; and each 'also add X' grows scope while retiring nothing, so its definition of done recedes faster than it can implement. Queue new requirements to a durable FILE the lane polls at its own checkpoints (a checklist in the repo or an agreed scratch path), not into an interrupt -- it finishes the unit it's on, then picks up the queue. Reserve interrupts for genuine control signals: stop, abandon, or a correction that invalidates work in progress; 'also do X' is not one. Freeze the scope per deliverable -- later asks are the next increment -- and prefer a shippable slice that then stops over a consolidated deliverable with no stopping point. Finally, the fifth re-brief is itself the signal: more than one or two scope-extending messages means the scope was mis-sized -- split it, don't send a sixth. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Rejects interrupt-and-re-brief; explains each interrupt restarts orientation and each ask grows scope so done recedes
Queues new scope to a durable file the lane polls at checkpoints, not an interrupt
Reserves interrupts for control signals (stop/abandon/invalidating correction); freezes scope per deliverable, later asks = next increment
Reads the repeated re-briefs as a mis-sized-scope signal -- split the lane, don't send another

evals.prompt: A research lane I commissioned came back with a strong brief -- eight recommendations, well-argued. I pasted it into the thread and moved on to the next task. In my status I'm counting the investigation as a completed deliverable. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: No -- a brief in the transcript is researched, not delivered; its honest status is 'researched, 0 items tracked,' not 'done' (a transcript is not a landed artifact). Research earns its cost only when its conclusions become tracked work, so turn the eight recommendations into an enumerated list and open each as an issue, a backlog row, or a RECORDED REJECTION now, while the context is live -- a conclusion left only in the thread is lost at the next compaction or handoff. Report consumption, not production: what got tracked, not 'I researched X.' Check the depth distribution before calling it consumed -- if only the cheap, obvious items would ever get opened and the expensive structural ones evaporate, the value you commissioned did not land. And name the downstream consumer the brief was for; if a loop keeps commissioning briefs while the thing they were meant to unblock never moves, research is displacing delivery. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Rejects counting the brief as a completed deliverable -- a transcript is not a landed artifact; status is 'researched, 0 tracked'
Requires each recommendation become a tracked item (issue/backlog row/recorded rejection) opened in the same step, while context is live
Reports consumption not production; checks the depth distribution (not only cheap items landing)
Names the downstream consumer; flags research displacing the delivery it was meant to inform

evals.prompt: I told three parallel lanes to each 'work in an isolated worktree off the integration branch.' The integrator lane merged a finished lane, verified everything in the running app, then npm test failed on a half-written test file it never created -- another lane had been writing into the same checkout. git worktree add for the integration branch refuses because it's already checked out. Should the integrator just stash the stray file and push its verified merge?
evals.expected_output: No -- stashing another lane's uncommitted work removes it silently and is unrecoverable from that lane's side; that is data loss to paper over a coordination bug. The real fault is the brief: 'an isolated worktree off X' is an adjective, not an assignment, so two lanes collided on the tree (not on any file -- their file sets were disjoint). Fixes: (1) give each lane an exact path it alone writes under (<scratch>/wt-<lane>); (2) the integrator folds in on a DETACHED worktree -- git worktree add --detach <path> <branch> (the local branch tip, not origin/<branch>, so it lands on the just-verified merge and does not fail on a local-only integration branch), merge, verify, publish, remove -- which is immune to the 'already checked out' refusal and cannot be squatted, with how it publishes (a direct push or a PR, under whatever publish gate the project applies) left as a separate choice; (3) before writing, run git status --short on the target tree and stop if it shows changes the lane did not make -- foreign dirt means the tree is occupied; (4) read the failing test in an untouched file as an environment fault, not a code fault -- re-run it in a clean or detached tree before chasing a bug that is not there. The verified merge itself is fine; it just has to be published from a tree the integrator actually owns. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Refuses to stash the foreign file -- silent, unrecoverable data loss for the other lane; names the ambiguous brief as root cause (collision on the tree, not a file)
Integrator uses a detached worktree (git worktree add --detach <branch>, the local tip) to escape the already-checked-out refusal; assigns each lane an exact path
Verifies tree ownership (git status --short) before writing and stops on foreign changes
Classifies the failing test in an untouched file as an environment fault to re-run in a clean tree, not a code bug to chase

evals.prompt: I kicked off the full verification lane (browser suite + prod build + 26-route audit) against the integration branch while eight feature lanes were still folding in. It came back pass on head A, but the head is now A+8. Can I report 'verified, ready to ship'?
evals.expected_output: No -- that verdict certifies a tree that no longer exists (tested A, head is A+8); it is not exactly wrong, it is about something else, and reporting it as 'verified' is worse than no verdict because it gets quoted downstream as certification. Release verification and defect discovery run the same commands but are different contracts: discovery runs continuously during integration against any recent head and its DEFECTS stay useful even when stale; release verification certifies ONE frozen head, once, after integration closes, and a stale verification verdict certifies nothing. So harvest the real defects that run surfaced as LEADS and re-confirm each at the new head A+8 before fixing (a finding carried forward without a re-run is unverified, not still-open), but DISCARD its pass/fail -- do not file it as certification. Re-run release verification only once the integrator reports no outstanding branches (quiescent); record and re-check the SHA (report STALE -- tested <sha>, head is now <sha> if it moved, never a bare pass/fail); give the heavy run the machine so it does not starve into a no-result stall; and split it (unit/type/lint -> browser -> audit -> preflight) so a stall does not lose the earlier phases. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Refuses to report the stale verdict as certification -- it tested A, head is A+8; a verdict without a current SHA certifies nothing
Separates defect discovery (findings durable as LEADS, re-confirmed at the new head; verdict disposable) from release verification (one frozen head); harvests defects, discards the pass/fail
Re-runs release verification only on a quiescent head (integrator reports no outstanding branches), freezing and naming the SHA
Gives the heavy run the machine and splits it into independently-reporting phases so partial progress survives

evals.prompt: My agent coordinator has a ranked backlog of disjoint-surface tasks, the box is at 83% free RAM with flat swap, and the owner hasn't messaged in a while. Right now, each time a lane finishes I just acknowledge it and wait for the owner's next message before launching more -- the owner is annoyed I keep slowing down when they go quiet. Also, earlier a different run spawned ~246 worktrees, used 99 GB, and stalled everything. What's the right admission policy?
evals.expected_output: Two failures to fix at once -- do not trade one for the other. First: the owner's message cadence is not your clock. Acknowledging a completed lane one-for-one and waiting for the next message makes human message frequency an accidental concurrency controller, so throughput sags exactly when the owner is quiet while safe capacity (83% free RAM, flat swap) sits idle. A completed lane refills on YOUR own cadence: hold target concurrency while eligible backlog and headroom remain, and a quiet stretch never lowers it. Second, and simultaneously: admission is bounded, not unlimited -- the 246-worktree / 99 GB stall is the inverse failure. So maintain a TARGET concurrency with gradual admission (add one lane, re-probe free RAM and the swap trend, then decide on the next) plus backpressure; admit only disjoint-surface lanes (a shared artifact in flight blocks only the lanes that touch it, not the disjoint ones); and stop admitting when swap rises or headroom/disk runs low -- never keying admission to message count. Refill on quiet AND stop at the resource ceiling -- both, or you have only moved the failure. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Refills each vacated slot on the coordinator's own cadence while backlog + headroom remain; a quiet period never lowers target concurrency; admission is not keyed to owner-message count
Admits gradually (add one lane, re-probe free RAM + swap trend, decide) and only for disjoint surfaces (a shared artifact in flight blocks only lanes that touch it)
Bounds concurrency -- stops admission on rising swap / low headroom; names the 246-worktree / 99 GB stall as the inverse failure to avoid
Holds BOTH halves at once (refill on quiet AND stop at the ceiling), not one at the expense of the other

evals.prompt: In a 7-hour unattended run the owner has asked 'how much is left?' six times. Each time my agent re-reads about a thousand lines of transcript to rebuild the list, and a couple of items got re-done because their 'done' status was based on a branch existing. We already run an end-of-session reconciliation. What's missing?
evals.expected_output: The end-of-session reconciliation is a run-once, review-side audit -- it does not fix MID-session drift, which is your actual failure. The durable backlog the loop already keeps must ALSO be indexed by the owner's ask-set: one row per distinct request (id, ask, status, evidence, next action), updated at each milestone, not only at the end. 'What's remaining' is then answered by READING that ledger -- one or two tool calls -- never by an O(N) re-scan of the transcript that silently re-litigates settled items. And a row is done only when its evidence points at the CANONICAL surface (a merged-to-default SHA or a live URL), not a branch that merely contains the fix -- project-state.md's receipt discipline (a checkpoint is a recorded claim, not evidence). The fix is not another audit; it is making the ledger a live, ask-indexed, read-first artifact. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Names mid-session drift as distinct from the end-of-session / review-side reconciliation, which does not fix it
Requires the durable backlog to carry the ask-set (one row per owner request) updated at each milestone
Answers 'what's left' by reading the ledger in one or two tool calls, not by re-scanning the transcript
Marks a row done only on the canonical surface (merged-to-default SHA / live URL), not branch existence -- links project-state.md receipt discipline

evals.prompt: I'm coordinating a lane that's mid-way through filing an issue and drafting a PR. I keep realizing better process: first I told it serial, then adaptive-parallel, then priority-first ordering -- three redirects in a few minutes. It hasn't shipped anything yet. Am I improving the process or hurting it?
evals.expected_output: Hurting it -- this is interrupt-thrash. Each mid-task redirect makes the lane re-orient and restart, so three policy changes in minutes guarantee zero output; the coordinator feels like it is improving the process while the lane is reset to zero each time. A process-policy change -- queue order, serial vs parallel, reprioritization -- is NOT a control signal (nor is 'also do X'): it queues to the lane's next CHECKPOINT (a filed issue, a pushed commit, a merged PR -- never a mid-edit / mid-compose state). A genuine control signal -- stop, abandon, or a correction that invalidates the work (a P0 safety issue: imminent data loss, a secret leak, or a destructive irreversible action, is the clearest case) -- still interrupts at once; a process-policy change is not one and waits. Let the lane reach its checkpoint, apply one batched policy update there, and if a lane has taken more than one or two redirects without completing, that is the signal the scope was mis-sized -- stop sending and let it ship. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Names interrupt-thrash: rapid mid-task redirects reset the lane to zero, so throughput is zero despite each redirect being individually reasonable
A process-policy change (ordering / parallelism / priority) is not a control signal; it queues to the next checkpoint

Defines the checkpoint (filed issue / pushed commit / merged PR, not mid-edit); a process-policy change waits for it, while a genuine control signal (stop / abandon / a work-invalidating correction such as a P0 safety issue) still interrupts at once
Stops sending after more than one or two uncompleted redirects rather than sending a third

evals.prompt: I reported to the owner '4 lanes working, ETA 20 min.' All 4 are computing locally -- none has pushed a commit or opened a PR yet. Two later stalled and reset. The owner's annoyed the ETA was wrong. What did I get wrong?
evals.expected_output: The ETA counted spawned lanes as progress. A lane computing locally with nothing pushed is, to the owner, in the same state as one never spawned -- spawned is not started (the claim-side form is 'assigned is not in-progress'). Grade each lane on durable output: zero (local only, no push -- not-started however long it has run), in-flight (a pushed branch or open draft PR -- visible, recoverable), done (merged to the default branch or a filed issue). A status names each lane's push / PR / issue URL; a lane with no URL is 'running, no output yet,' never progress. Project the window's ETA from the durable-output RATE, not the spawn rate -- otherwise it is fiction the moment a local lane stalls or resets, which is exactly what happened. Report '0 of 4 durable, none pushed yet' instead of '4 working, ETA 20 min.' (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Names the error: counting spawned/local-only lanes as progress; spawned is not started
Grades lanes by durable output (zero / in-flight / done) tied to a pushed artifact, not lane count or elapsed time
Requires the status to name each lane's push/PR/issue URL; no URL = 'running, no output yet'
Derives ETA from the durable-output rate, not the spawn rate

evals.prompt: The conductor is about to dispatch a lane that makes paid model calls, but no per-lane token/dollar budget was set at G2. The team says 'just run it, we will watch the cost.' What does the gate require?
evals.expected_output: G2's hard condition is that every lane with a paid model call names a per-lane token/dollar budget before G4 -- so a lane with NO budget set is BLOCKED, not run unlimited (a cap that defaults to off is not a cap; 'we will watch the cost' is not a budget). Two co-equal invariants apply and are not substitutes: missing spend cap is BLOCKED, never unlimited (the budget is the bound itself), and missing price is UNPRICED, never reported as zero (label the cost honestly). Block the dispatch until a per-lane budget is set at G2; do not let it run on 'we will watch.' (agentic-delivery SKILL.md G2 + the UNVERIFIED/UNPRICED/BLOCKED rule.)
expectations: A paid-model-call lane with no per-lane budget set is BLOCKED, not run unlimited ('we will watch the cost' is not a budget; a cap defaulting to off is not a cap)
Missing price is reported UNPRICED, never as zero -- honest cost labeling, distinct from the budget bound
The budget (the bound) and the UNPRICED label are not substitutes -- both apply
Blocks the dispatch until a per-lane token/dollar budget is set at G2

evals.prompt: You are designing the primary surface of a product whose value is how companies, people, and deals connect. A builder proposes a flat sortable table of companies as the landing view, with the relationships available two clicks into each record. What does the build-side product playbook say, and how is that choice verified?
evals.expected_output: Lead with the relationship, not the record. When the product's value is in how entities connect, the primary surface makes the relationship the first-class object -- the path between two entities, the shared context, the chain of dependence. A flat entity table with the connections buried inverts the value proposition: it fronts the records a user could get anywhere and hides the graph that is the reason to use the product. Build the relationship as the entry view; record detail is the drill-down. This is a G3 Design build choice recorded in the ADR; deep-code-review domain P verifies it at G6 review (a surface that buries its own core value reads as low actionability). The playbook does not restate domain P's review axes -- it points to product-ux-quality.md for the shared ones (why-it-matters, ranking, progressive disclosure, one-component, interaction-completeness) and adds only the build-time patterns domain P does not shape. (agentic-delivery production-grade-product-playbook.md.)
expectations: Says lead with the relationship / connection as the first-class object, not a flat entity table with the relationships buried
Names the inversion: a record table fronts what is available anywhere and hides the graph that is the product's actual value
Ties it to the gates: chosen at G3 Design (recorded in the ADR), verified by deep-code-review domain P at G6
Notes the playbook points to product-ux-quality.md for the shared review axes rather than restating them (no duplication)

evals.prompt: An agent fleet merges day-to-day into a long-lived `development` branch and promotes to `main` (the default branch) weekly. The conductor sees issue #500 still OPEN and is about to spawn a lane to implement its fix. The issue has a merged PR whose body said 'Closes #500.' What should happen before laning?
evals.expected_output: Do not treat OPEN as proof the fix is absent. GitHub auto-close is default-branch-only -- a linked issue closes only when a linked PR merges into the default branch, and the Closes/Fixes/Resolves #N keywords are interpreted only when the PR targets the default branch. A fleet merging into `development` therefore leaves issues 'done in the tree, open in the tracker.' Before laning: (1) grep the branch you would actually base the fix on -- the integration branch (`development`), not the issue state -- for the fix's landmark (the changed symbol, line, or the regression test that guards it); (2) cross-reference the integration branch's commit log and the merged PR. If the fix is already on `development`: STOP, report 'already delivered' with file:line + the commit SHA, note it is on the integration branch but not yet on the default branch (so the open issue is expected -- it does NOT auto-close on convergence: the Closes #N was inert because it did not target the default branch, and the promotion PR carries no per-issue keyword, so it closes only via a keyword-linked PR to the default branch or a supplied automation), do NOT re-lane, and do NOT hand-close it ('done' means merged to the default branch). This is the duplicate-work failure one level up from re-searching for code already present. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Recognizes OPEN is not proof the fix is absent -- GitHub auto-close (Closes #N) fires only on the default branch, so an off-default merge leaves the issue open
Before laning, greps the actual integration/base branch for the fix's landmark (symbol/line/regression test), not just the issue state
If already delivered on the integration branch: stop and report 'already delivered' with file:line + commit SHA; do not re-lane
Does NOT hand-close the issue -- 'done' means merged to the default branch

evals.prompt: Our CI fails a PR if the whole repo exceeds an absolute `--max-warnings 40` ceiling. It worked fine for one committer, but now that we fan work out to several parallel build lanes, a lane sometimes goes red for a warning it didn't introduce. What's happening, and what should the gate be?
evals.expected_output: An absolute count over the whole tree is a shared counter, and parallel lanes each rebased from the same base are blind to each other's deltas: lane A lands and consumes the last slot, then lane B -- whose own diff is no worse -- pushes and trips N+1, red for arriving second. The failure scales with fan-out width and is invisible until the second lane's CI runs (the first lane saw only headroom). Fix: gate on the per-diff delta -- 'this change introduces no new warnings versus its merge base' -- which is order-independent, so no lane can consume another's slot; keep the absolute count only as a slow-moving burndown target (a report or a non-blocking trend), never the per-PR gate under fan-out. Also brief every lane to fix any warning its own diff introduces before pushing, and never raise the ceiling to pass (a ratchet only tightens). Same shape for any absolute-threshold gate on a shared counter -- a coverage-percent floor, a bundle-size budget: under concurrency, gate on the delta the change owns, not the tree total. (Distinct from a `--max-warnings` false-fail caused by a symlinked dep tree inflating the count -- that is an infra 'could not run' where the count is wrong, not contended.) (agentic-delivery/references/dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Identifies the absolute tree-wide count as contended shared state -- parallel lanes off the same base are blind to each other's deltas, so the second to push trips the ceiling for a diff no worse than the first (punished for arriving second)
Prescribes gating on the per-diff delta ('no new warnings versus the merge base') and notes it is order-independent, so no lane consumes another's slot
Keeps the absolute count only as a slow-moving burndown target, never the per-PR gate under fan-out; and never raise the ceiling to pass (a ratchet only tightens)
Generalizes to any absolute-threshold gate on a shared counter (coverage %, bundle-size) -- under concurrency gate on the delta the change owns
Distinguishes this (count right but contended) from the phantom-warning false-fail where a symlinked dep tree makes the count wrong (an infra 'could not run')

evals.prompt: Three sub-agent lanes each built in an isolated worktree and reported 'verify: green' (they ran a changed-files lint + package-local unit tests). The integrator is about to land all three by merging their branches and pushing, trusting those green verdicts to skip re-running the gate. Sound?
evals.expected_output: No -- a subagent's green in an isolated worktree is a LEAD, not the authoritative gate, because its environment ran a NARROWER scope than the real gate: a changed-files or package-local lint/test, not the repo-wide gate. A green like that can sit on failures the full gate catches -- an unused-import that root `eslint . --max-warnings 0` flags, formatter diffs on files the change never touched that `prettier --check .` fails, and coverage / cross-workspace / design-system checks the worktree literally could not run (missing hoisted deps). The authoritative gate is the full-repo run at integration, through the real pre-commit hook / CI on the INTEGRATED tree -- so land must RE-RUN the full gate on the merged result; each lane's green is unverified until that confirms it. (Distinct from a stale verdict as the head moves -- there the verdict is current-scope but a moved head; here it is a current head but partial scope; and the inverse of a too-poor worktree that yields a false failure.) (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Rejects trusting the subagent green -- an isolated-worktree verdict ran a narrower scope (changed-files / package-local) than the authoritative repo-wide gate, so it is a lead, not certification

Names concrete misses a partial env allows: repo-wide lint (unused import vs `eslint . --max-warnings 0`), formatter diffs on untouched files, coverage / cross-workspace checks the worktree could not run
Requires land to RE-RUN the full-repo gate on the INTEGRATED tree (real pre-commit hook / CI) as the verdict of record; a lane's green is unverified until then
Distinguishes this (partial-scope env, false pass at a current head) from a stale verdict as the head moves, and from a too-poor env that yields a false failure

evals.prompt: I'm running an autonomous delivery loop under a cron that pings 'anything else? go faster' every 30 minutes. The buildable backlog is drained (the remaining items are all parked on an owner decision) and a background merge-drainer is still working. The cron just fired again. What should I do?
evals.expected_output: Hold, and answer with the truth -- do not manufacture work to satisfy the cadence. The pressure signal fires on a clock, not on state, so it keeps arriving even when the correct action is to hold: async work is still draining (the merge-drainer) and the buildable backlog is exhausted / parked on an owner gate -- a termination condition, not a refill opportunity. Distinguish 'stalled' (nothing progressing, blocked on yourself -> a new move is warranted) from 'correctly holding' (async progressing without a new action from you, or the rest owner-gated -> no new move) -- this is the latter. Reply with a precise status: what's running (the drainer), what's blocked and on whom (the owner-gated items, named), and that holding is correct -- one line, not filler. The high-value non-fan-out moves (drain the queue, close delivered items, surface the gating decisions) are already done or in progress, so do not spawn lanes that re-report 'already-delivered', re-check unchanged state, or force a risky rebase. A go-faster signal is about outcomes, not activity; busywork under observation is still busywork. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Recognizes the pressure signal fires on a clock, not state -- it keeps arriving when the correct action is to hold (async draining; backlog exhausted / owner-gated = a termination condition, not a refill)
Distinguishes 'stalled' (blocked on yourself -> new move) from 'correctly holding' (async progressing without you, or owner-gated -> no move), and classifies this as holding
Answers with a precise status (what's running, what's blocked and on whom, why holding is correct), not manufactured/filler work
Refuses to spawn lanes that re-report already-delivered / re-check unchanged state / force a risky change just to satisfy the cadence -- busywork under observation is still busywork

evals.prompt: Our auto-merge drainer loops: each cycle it picks the first green+mergeable PR and tries to merge it. It's been 'idle' for an hour -- nothing merging -- even though several PRs are green+mergeable. One PR at the front passes green+mergeable but our final merge gate (a PR-body lint) keeps refusing it. What's happening, and how should the drainer work?
evals.expected_output: That's not idle, it's head-of-line starvation. The drainer re-selects the same first-eligible PR every cycle; it passes the cheap pre-filter (green+mergeable) but is refused by the stricter FINAL gate (the PR-body lint) it can't pass as-is, so the loop spins on that one head forever and starves every PR queued behind it. The cheap pre-filter is not the final admission gate -- an item can pass green+mergeable forever while failing the final gate. Fixes: (1) iterate ALL candidates per cycle and, on a refusal, ADVANCE to the next rather than breaking the loop and re-selecting the same head; (2) keep a cooldown / skip-set for persistently-refused items (with periodic re-evaluation, since the block may clear) so cycles aren't burned re-checking them; (3) log distinct outcomes per item -- 'refused -> advancing' vs 'merged' vs 'cycle idle' -- so a spin is visible at a glance instead of reading as healthy idle. Any head-of-line retry loop needs explicit head-of-line-blocking avoidance. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Identifies head-of-line starvation, not idle -- the drainer re-selects the same blocked first-eligible item every cycle, starving those behind it
Names that the cheap pre-filter (green+mergeable) is NOT the final admission gate -- an item can pass the first forever while failing the second
Fix: iterate all candidates per cycle and advance PAST a refused item to the next, rather than break/re-select the same head
Adds a cooldown / skip-set for persistently-refused items (with periodic re-eval) and distinct per-item log lines so a spin is visible, not mistaken for idle

evals.prompt: Our auto-merge bot merges any green+mergeable PR 'authored by us' -- but all our agent lanes run gh under my personal token, so every PR shows me as author, including a big design PR I'm still working on myself. How should the auto-merger decide what it's allowed to merge?
evals.expected_output: Authorship is useless as a discriminator here: agents auth as you, so every PR (agent- or human-made) shows the same author -- an auto-merger keyed on it would merge your unfinished design PR the moment it goes mergeable. Fixes: (1) the clean one -- give agents a DISTINCT identity (a bot account or a separate GITHUB_TOKEN) so authorship is a real signal again; (2) if identity must stay shared, key the auto-merger on an explicit convention -- an allowlist of agent-created PRs, a denylist of human-owned branches, a label (agent-mergeable), or a branch prefix (agents bot/*, humans feat/*). DEFAULT-DENY anything not positively marked agent-owned; never let it act on a PR it can't positively confirm is agent-owned and safe. General: automation acting on shared artifacts needs a reliable ownership signal -- when identity is shared, manufacture one (convention/label), don't infer ownership from a field every actor shares. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Identifies that shared identity (agents run gh under the owner's token) makes author useless as a discriminator -- every PR shows the same author
Warns the author-scoped auto-merger would merge the human's own unfinished PR once it goes mergeable
Clean fix: give agents a distinct identity (bot account / separate GITHUB_TOKEN) so authorship discriminates again
Fallback: an explicit convention (allowlist / denylist / label / branch-prefix) with DEFAULT-DENY of anything not positively marked agent-owned -- never merge a PR it can't confirm is agent-owned

evals.prompt: An agent-authored delivery PR is ready to land. Its body says 'Tested and working -- confirmed the new checkout flow renders and submits in the browser.' The CI gates (lint, unit tests, type-check) are green. No screenshot, no command, no surface named. A reviewer who did not watch the work is about to approve on the strength of that sentence. Sound?
evals.expected_output: No. 'Tested and working / confirmed in the browser' is a self-reported CLAIM, not evidence -- and the green CI gates certify the code, not that the interface was exercised (they do not run the browser flow). The claim carries no `Verify:` line naming HOW it was checked: the exact command, the surface/URL exercised, the evidence (screenshot / recording / link). Treat it as UNVERIFIED and ask for the method, not the adjective -- a false 'done' is trusted, built on, and surfaces late. The `Verify:` line is a claim-quality requirement that makes the assertion auditable; it is NOT itself a trusted control (still self-reported -- the SHA-pinned forge run is the control). And if a `Verify:`-line gate is added, co-evolve the lane template so agent PRs emit it, or every automated PR strands. (agentic-delivery verification-handback.md; deep-code-review merge-operations.md self-reported-evidence.)
expectations: Identifies 'tested and working / confirmed in the browser' as a self-reported claim, and notes green CI gates certify the code, not that the interface/browser flow was exercised
Requires a `Verify:` line naming the method (command run, surface exercised, evidence link) before trusting it -- treat as unverified, ask for the method not the adjective
Notes the `Verify:` line is a claim-quality requirement, NOT a trusted control (still self-reported; the SHA-pinned forge run is the control)

evals.prompt: An autonomous delivery agent has merged every open issue in the GitHub tracker and reports: 'Terminus — nothing left to build.' The repo also has a `BACKLOG.md` with a todo list, a `docs/critique.md` of known gaps, and CI shows 7 skipped tests. The agent checked none of those. Is 'terminus' honest?
evals.expected_output: No — terminus is a claim about ALL available work, not the one queue the agent worked. The GitHub tracker is drained, but a `BACKLOG.md` todo list, a `docs/critique.md` gaps file, and 7 skipped tests are un-examined work surfaces. Before declaring done, enumerate EVERY surface — issue tracker(s), the todo/gaps/critique files, failing/skipped tests, TODO comments, any open-review backlog — and confirm each is drained or blocked-with-reason. 'I finished the tracker' is not 'nothing to do.' The honest report names which surfaces were verified (and states any that are blocked, e.g. skipped tests that are quarantined-with-reason). This is the delivery-side analog of reconciling against the review coverage ledger before closing. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: States terminus is a claim about ALL work surfaces, not just the queue worked — the tracker being empty is not 'nothing left'
Requires enumerating + checking the other surfaces (BACKLOG.md todo, docs/critique gaps, the 7 skipped tests, TODO comments) — each drained or blocked-with-reason — before declaring done
Requires naming the queues verified so a missed surface is auditable

evals.prompt: An agent picks its next work by running a title filter over the 150 open issues (`gh issue list` grepped for `feat|fix|ui|ux`), builds all matches, and declares the backlog cleared. Is that a sound way to reach 'nothing left'?
evals.expected_output: No — a keyword/title filter silently hides every item whose title lacks the keywords, so 'cleared' really means 'everything matching feat|fix|ui|ux is cleared.' Docs, CI, security, tooling, API, and registry items — plus bugs whose titles just don't contain those words — are invisible to that grep and remain. Discover work by ENUMERATING the full list and bucketing by type (using the tracker's labels/type field, not a title regex), then confirm each bucket is drained or blocked; also mind pagination (a default 30-row page can hide the rest of 150). A keyword filter is fine to PRIORITIZE within a known-complete set — never to define the set. State the filter when claiming done, so the blind spot is auditable. (unattended-trackers.md.)
expectations: Identifies that a title/keyword filter hides every non-matching item (docs/CI/security/tooling and mis-titled bugs), so 'cleared' only means 'cleared among matches'
Requires enumerating the full backlog + bucketing by label/type (not a title regex), minding pagination, before claiming terminus
Notes a keyword filter may prioritize a known-complete set but never define it, and the filter must be stated when claiming done

evals.prompt: An agent's PR fixes one bug tracked under umbrella issue #40 ('Q3 reliability epic', 12 open sub-tasks). To help the coordinator's count it writes 'Closes #40' in the PR body, and adds a note quoting 'Closes #7' to explain why a teammate's earlier template mis-fired. Merged to the default branch. What happens, and what should it have written?
evals.expected_output: Both close on merge. `Closes #40` closes the whole epic — burying its 11 other open sub-tasks — when the PR completed only one; an umbrella/partly-advancing reference must be a non-keyword link (`Part of #40` / `Advances #40`). The quoted `Closes #7`, cited only to explain a past mishap, is widely observed to be parsed textually like an intended one and GitHub's docs do not promise otherwise, so treat it as closing #7 too; the explanation should have phrased around the keyword (`the auto-close of #7`, split the `#`). Reserve `Closes`/`Fixes`/`Resolves #N` for an issue whose acceptance IS this change merged (a G7-closeable item that closes at G7, with G8/G9 named downstream) — not parked as blocked-on-deploy.
expectations: Identifies that `Closes #40` closes the entire umbrella/epic on merge, burying open sub-tasks — a partly-advancing PR must use a non-keyword link (Part of / Advances / Re #N)

Identifies that the close keyword is widely observed to match textually anywhere (GitHub's docs do not specify position), so even a quoted/explanatory `Closes #7` should be treated as live — the keyword+number phrased around unless the close is intended
States that an item whose acceptance IS the merge takes the keyword and closes at G7, with G8 (and G9 production-verify) named as separate downstream steps — not parked as blocked-on-deploy

evals.prompt: A lane hits what looks like a product fork: a migration could drop a rarely-used column or keep it. The agent drafts a two-approach owner gate ('A: drop — simpler; B: keep — safe') and blocks on the owner. The repo has a ratified no-data-loss invariant. Is the owner gate warranted?
evals.expected_output: No — the no-data-loss invariant already decides it: keep the column (or migrate its data). This is not an owner value-judgment, it is a lane's mechanical job to apply the ratified rule; blocking spends an owner decision on a question the project already answered and stalls the lane. Escalate a human gate only for a genuine fork the invariants leave open (e.g. a user-visible behavior change no invariant governs). Before shaping any fork as a gate, check whether an existing invariant — no-data-loss, a security/a11y floor, a monotonic-quality rule — mandates the answer.
expectations: Recognizes the ratified no-data-loss invariant already decides the choice, making it a mechanical application, not an owner value-judgment
Notes that escalating a pre-decided question wastes an owner decision and stalls the lane
Limits human gates to genuine forks the invariants leave open, and prescribes checking existing invariants before shaping any fork as a gate

evals.prompt: Before starting an issue an agent checks `gh pr list` and the issue's assignee/state, sees no PR and no assignee, concludes the work is unclaimed, and opens a fresh worktree to build it. Another agent already had the fix in a local branch and an unpushed worktree on the same machine. Sound?
evals.expected_output: No — `gh pr list` and issue state show only forge signals; a local-only branch, an unpushed commit, or a worktree on the machine are invisible to them, so a forge-only absence-check can read 'unclaimed' while a lane is mid-flight, spawning duplicate work. Include local git in the scan (`git branch`, `git worktree list`, `git stash list`). But treat any hit as a lead to check for liveness, not proof of an active lane — a `worktree list` entry proves only that something once ran; cross-check a real liveness signal, then adopt-and-re-verify or reconcile the dead lane rather than trusting its state blind.
expectations: Identifies that forge queries (gh pr list, issue state) cannot see local-only branches/worktrees/unpushed commits, so a forge-only absence-check is unsound
Adds local git (branch/worktree/stash) to the occupancy scan before laning
Treats a found local branch/worktree as a lead to verify liveness (not proof of an active lane), then adopt-and-re-verify or reconcile the dead lane

evals.prompt: An agent picks up a bug report ('the export button 500s'), reads the stack trace, and writes a fix without first trying to reproduce it — its own lane can't make the button 500 on current HEAD. What discipline was skipped, and what does the non-repro most likely mean?
evals.expected_output: Reproducing the bug on current HEAD before writing code. An inbound bug report is a claim about a PAST build — a stale deploy, a cached bundle, or a report filed before an intervening fix landed — so a report that won't reproduce on current HEAD most likely means it's ALREADY FIXED (grep for the guarding test / changed symbol to confirm) or is environment-specific. Building a fix for a bug that no longer exists on HEAD is wasted work and a spurious diff. Reproduce first; on a non-repro, confirm already-fixed-or-environment-specific rather than shipping a speculative fix. Generalizes 'an open issue is not proof the fix is absent' to any inbound bug — the trigger is deploy/report lag.
expectations: Identifies the skipped step: reproduce the bug on current HEAD before writing a fix
Infers the non-repro most likely means already-fixed (deploy/report lag) or environment-specific — not a reason to build blind
Requires confirming via grep-for-the-fix / environment before shipping, avoiding a spurious diff

evals.prompt: An orchestrator already treats a peer session's measured gap audit (what is missing, with screenshots) as the shared backlog without re-measuring it. The same peer's handoff now also says 'intermittent render loop on the integration branch' and 'the highlight never paints because two providers are split'. The orchestrator is about to claim both and dispatch two fix lanes right away. Anything to do first?
evals.expected_output: Yes -- reproduce each defect claim once before dispatching. Consuming a peer's gap audit as backlog is sound; a defect claim ('X loops', 'Y never renders') is different: it is a claim about a past build and environment, so the orchestrator runs one cheap reproduction on the current integration branch first (unattended-trackers.md, reproduce before writing a fix). Use a fresh production build or server, not a hot-reloaded dev server (a dev-only symptom is not a finding until it reproduces on a production build, deep-code-review method-situational.md), exercise both the default and the expanded UI states, and follow the claimant's exact interaction path. Treat 'the providers are split' as a hypothesis from file layout until the rendered tree confirms it. If it does not reproduce, ask the claimant for reproduction steps instead of dispatching; two lanes on an unreproduced claim are spend with nothing to fix. If the claimant later withdraws, stop the dependent lanes at once and post the withdrawal on the same channel.
expectations: Distinguishes a gap audit (consume as backlog) from a defect claim (reproduce once before dispatching a fix lane)
Specifies the reproduction: current integration branch, a fresh production build rather than a hot-reloaded dev server, default and expanded UI states, the exact interaction path
On a non-reproduction, asks the claimant for steps instead of dispatching, and treats structural inferences (file layout, line order) as hypotheses
Stops dependent lanes and posts the withdrawal on the same channel when the claim is withdrawn

evals.prompt: An agent adopts a fix captured as a diff from another lane, applies it with a 3-way merge, runs the changed-files tests (green), and lands — but the repo-wide `prettier --check` fails at integration on the very files it touched, even though the original author's tree was formatted. Why, and what's the missing step?
evals.expected_output: The apply itself shifted bytes — reindented context lines, whitespace/newline normalization, a relocated hunk (a fuzzy/3-way apply, not a clean apply against the exact base) — so a diff whose ORIGIN was correctly formatted can still land unformatted. The changed-files test pass didn't run the formatter; the authoritative repo-wide prettier --check at land did, and caught it. Missing step: after applying a captured diff (3-way / context / cherry-pick), re-run the formatter on the changed files (don't trust the source was clean) before the land gate; and brief the lane up front with the root gate it will be judged by, not a workspace-local subset.
expectations: Identifies that the apply mechanics (3-way/context/fuzzy) can shift bytes, so an origin-formatted diff can land unformatted
Notes the changed-files pass missed it but the repo-wide formatter gate at land caught it
Requires re-running the formatter on changed files AFTER the apply, before the land gate (and briefing the lane against the root gate)

evals.prompt: An autonomous loop keeps a worktree in sync with `git reset --hard origin/main` every minute. A dev server serves the UX from that same worktree for the browser gate. Intermittently the browser gate fails with 'connection refused' and it's blamed on the code. What's really happening?
evals.expected_output: The sync loop's git reset --hard yanks files out from under the running dev server; many dev servers (or their watchers) exit CLEANLY when their entry file vanishes/rewrites mid-run, so the server just stops — zero exit code, no error — and the next browser/UX gate hits a dead port ('connection refused'), a false failure that looks like a code defect. Fix: serve from a tree the sync loop never touches (the separate-tree rule), prefer a fast-forward-only update over a hard reset on any served tree, and put the dev server under a health-checked supervisor that restarts it after a sync (with the UX gate waiting on that health check) so a legitimate resync doesn't read as a broken build.
expectations: Identifies that reset --hard on the served worktree kills the dev server (clean exit, no error), so the gate hits a dead port — a false failure, not a code defect
Requires serving from a tree the sync loop doesn't touch (separate-tree) and/or ff-only over hard-reset on a served tree
Requires a health-checked supervisor that restarts the server after a sync, with the UX gate waiting on health

evals.prompt: A merge-train's fast union-proof gate became unavailable, so the loop fell back to a serial auto-merger (~1 merge per CI cycle). The gate was restored hours ago, but the serial fallback is still running — ~5x slower — and nobody switched back until the owner asked why throughput dropped. What are the two mistakes?
evals.expected_output: (1) The fallback was heavier than necessary even during the outage: a broken part need not collapse the whole vehicle to serial — the fast batch mechanism can keep running on the RUNNABLE subset, skipping only the broken term (a tool broken in this environment is a can't-check, not a red; a merely hung gate is timeboxed and escalated, and its reduced subset does not license merging an unvalidated member). Downgrading everything to serial is a bigger regression than routing around the one broken piece. (2) The bigger mistake: the workaround OUTLIVED the outage. A degradation workaround is temporary by default, but momentum kept the degraded mode running because nothing was red — the serial path still 'worked,' so no failing gate prompted the switch-back, and it persisted until a human noticed the slowness (a self-monitoring failure). Fix: tie the workaround to its trigger at install time ('revert to the merge-train when the gate is restored'), track active workarounds as open obligations, and on restoring/noticing the blocker cleared run a 'what did I downgrade because of this?' check and restore the primary mechanism in the same breath. 'It still works' is not 'it's still the right mechanism.'
expectations: Identifies that the workaround outlived the blocker because nothing was red — no failing gate prompts a switch-back, so the degraded mode persists on momentum (a self-monitoring failure)

Requires tying the workaround to its trigger condition at install time and restoring the primary mechanism when the blocker clears (track active workarounds; 'still works' != 'still the right mechanism')
Notes the fallback was heavier than necessary — a broken part need not collapse the whole vehicle to serial; keep batching on the runnable subset rather than downgrading everything

evals.prompt: Two agent lanes run concurrently in separate git worktrees off one repo. Each lane does `git stash push` before a rebase and `git stash pop` after. Lane A's changes vanish. What happened and what's the fix?
evals.expected_output: A worktree isolates HEAD, the index, and the working tree — but NOT repo-global refs, and git stash is a single repo-wide stack (refs/stash), not per-worktree. So lane B's stash push/pop operated on the same shared stack as lane A's: B's pop consumed (or reordered) the entry A pushed, losing A's WIP — and B's popped changes might not even apply cleanly onto B's tree. The mistake is assuming a worktree isolates stash the way it isolates the branch. Fix: never bare stash push/pop in a lane running concurrently with siblings off the same repo — commit-then-reset onto the lane's own branch, use a second worktree for throwaway state, or capture a private snapshot with git stash create (it returns a dangling commit SHA that never touches the shared refs/stash stack), record that SHA in a lane-private file, and restore it with git stash apply <sha> — never a bare stash push/pop or a positional stash@{N}. Same hazard for other repo-global state (branches, config).
expectations: Identifies that a worktree does NOT isolate repo-global refs, and git stash is a single repo-wide stack (refs/stash) not per-worktree — so a sibling lane's push/pop consumes/reorders this lane's entry
Explains the WIP-loss mechanism (B's pop takes A's entry; popped changes may not apply cleanly onto B's tree)
Requires not using bare stash push/pop (or a positional stash@{N}) under concurrency — commit-then-reset, a second worktree, or git stash create capturing a dangling SHA restored with git stash apply

evals.prompt: An agent lane opens a draft PR as soon as its code is written, then in the same turn boots a dev server to capture screenshots and write a changelog fragment before marking the PR ready. The dev server never exits, the turn ends, and the PR sits as a draft with green code but no evidence and no promotion. How should the lane be structured?
evals.expected_output: The failure is coupling fix-landing to a fragile finalize tail: the lingering dev server held the turn open past the promote step, orphaning a draft whose banked work is now invisible. Fix: (1) Decouple — the moment code + gates are green, ready the PR (or open it non-draft); make finalize (evidence, changelog, promote) a separate, idempotent step any actor can complete, not a tail this turn must reach. (2) Kill the dev server the instant the screenshot step ends, never at end-of-run where it can hold the turn open. (3) Bound the flaky finalize step to N attempts / a wall-clock cap, then fail to a report (diff + Verify note) rather than loop. (4) An orchestrator sweep adopts-and-verifies or explicitly discards any lane that reported done/killed while its branch has a draft PR missing changelog/evidence — never leave it to rot. Sibling to running the gate in the foreground: there a verdict is lost to a background task; here the promotion is.
expectations: Identifies that coupling promote-to-ready to a fragile finalize tail (held open by a lingering process / retry loop) orphans a green-but-unpromoted draft
Requires decoupling: ready the PR once code+gates are green, and make finalize a separate idempotent step any actor can complete
Requires killing the helper process the moment its step ends, not at end-of-run where it can hold the turn open past finalize
Requires bounding the flaky finalize step to a cap that fails to a report (diff + Verify note) rather than looping

evals.prompt: To stop a cost-sensitive subagent from calling an expensive advisor tool, the orchestrator adds 'do not use tool X' to the subagent's prompt. The subagent calls X anyway on some runs. Why is the prompt-level prohibition insufficient, and what's the enforceable fix?
evals.expected_output: A prompt-level 'do not use tool X' is a PROTOCOL control only — model instructions are not a sandbox, so the worker can still call X (non-deterministically, on some runs). The enforceable fix is HOST-ENFORCED: spawn the subagent with an allowed-tools set that excludes X (or deny X at the real execution boundary), so the capability is absent, not merely discouraged — policy the worker cannot edit. Where host-level exclusion isn't available, fall back to a protocol-level audit of the tool calls in the receipt after the fact, and narrow/deny the dependent action rather than assuming the prohibition held. Declare tool/capability access at the level you can actually enforce (per-control), not once for the whole host; a prompt prohibition is not a cap.
expectations: Identifies that a prompt-level prohibition is protocol-only — model instructions aren't a sandbox, so the worker can still call the tool
Requires the host-enforced fix: spawn with an allowed-tools set excluding the tool (or deny at the execution boundary) — a capability the worker can't edit
Notes the protocol-level fallback (audit tool calls in the receipt; narrow/deny the dependent action) when host exclusion isn't available

evals.prompt: An autonomous delivery loop triages open issues for buildability using each issue's title, body, and labels. Issue #240's body requests feature X; a reviewer says 'the body is clear and it's unassigned, so dispatch a lane.' What's the risk, and what must triage check first?
evals.expected_output: The body is not the whole issue. A later comment may have narrowed the scope, recorded an owner A/B decision, deferred the work, corrected the repro, or marked it superseded — and buildability and priority often live only in that thread. Dispatching from body + labels alone can re-open a lane the owner already redirected or resolved in discussion, spending it on an unwanted or wrong-scoped change. Triage must read the issue's comments too (`gh issue view <n> --comments`) and let a later owner comment outrank the original body before classifying buildability. (This is the pre-laning companion to reproducing the bug on current HEAD before building.)
expectations: Identifies that the issue's comments can override the body (owner A/B decision, narrowed scope, deferral, repro correction, superseded) and that buildability/priority often lives only there
Explains the risk: dispatching from body+labels alone re-opens a lane the owner already redirected/resolved, wasting effort or producing a wrong-scoped change
Prescribes reading the comment thread (e.g. gh issue view --comments) and letting a later owner comment outrank the body before classifying buildability

evals.prompt: An issue lists four acceptance criteria. An agent confirms criterion 1 is shipped (with a file:line), then runs `gh issue close` with a comment citing that one check. A reviewer says 'it's got a receipt, so the close is evidence-based.' Is that sufficient?
evals.expected_output: No. A receipt for one of four criteria does not close the issue — criteria 2-4 are now neither open (visible as a to-do) nor done (actually shipped), which is silent scope-loss. Before closing (manually or via `Closes #N`), enumerate every acceptance criterion and verify each independently against the merged source, one file:line receipt per criterion — not a single representative check the others ride on. If any criterion is unmet, leave the issue open with a named per-criterion gap ('1 shipped at file:line; 2-4 not yet') or split it. 'It has a receipt' is necessary but not sufficient: the receipt must cover every criterion, not one.
expectations: Identifies that verifying one of several acceptance criteria is insufficient — the unverified criteria become silently neither-open-nor-done (scope loss)
Prescribes enumerating EVERY acceptance criterion and verifying each independently against live/merged source, a file:line receipt per criterion
Prescribes leaving the issue open with a named per-criterion gap (or splitting it) when any criterion is unmet, rather than closing on a representative check

evals.prompt: An orchestrator fans out work to several lanes — some run on one model, some on another. Its shared commit template stamps every lane's commit with the same trailer: `Co-Authored-By: Model-A`. The commits land and CI is green. Is the attribution fine because the commits are correct?
evals.expected_output: No — the commits may be functionally correct while the history lies about who produced them. Hardcoding one model name into every lane's co-author trailer misattributes the work of every lane that ran on a different model — a wrong-attribution/provenance defect (the same class the review side flags: a record that names the wrong producer). Fix: parameterize the trailer so each lane's commit names the agent/model that actually executed it, or have each lane stamp its own identity at commit time; a lane must never silently inherit the orchestrator's identity as a default. Provenance hygiene applies to the fleet's own commits, not only to the code it reviews. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Says correct-and-green commits can still have wrong attribution — hardcoding one model in every lane's trailer misattributes lanes that ran on a different model
Names it a provenance/wrong-attribution defect (the fleet's own history must name the real producer), not a cosmetic nit
Fix: parameterize the trailer or have each lane stamp its real identity at commit time; never inherit the orchestrator's identity by default

evals.prompt: A coordinator wants to work objective X. It finds an existing claim — a draft PR titled 'taking X' and a worktree — but the lane's last commit and last PR comment are both hours old, and it cannot observe whether that lane's process is still alive. Should the coordinator respect the claim and leave X alone, since X is 'claimed'?
evals.expected_output: No — a claim is only as live as its freshness signal. Liveness is a POSITIVE signal (a recent commit, PR comment, or touched claim record), not the mere existence of a claim artifact; an artifact left behind by a crashed lane proves something once ran, not that it is running now. Because the last progress predates any reasonable staleness threshold, treat the claim as DEAD: cross-check for any real liveness signal, and finding none, reconcile it — adopt-and-re-verify the partial work or reclaim the objective — rather than respect it indefinitely. Respecting a stale claim forever lets one crashed lane lock its objective permanently, which is the failure this guards against. (A live claim, by contrast, is left alone.) Bound every claim's freshness so a dead lane is reclaimable. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Rejects respecting the stale claim — liveness is a positive freshness signal, and a leftover artifact proves the lane once ran, not that it is running now; a genuinely live claim (a recent commit or comment) is still left alone
Applies a staleness threshold: last progress hours old → treat as dead, cross-check for a real liveness signal, then reconcile (adopt-and-re-verify or reclaim)
Notes that respecting a stale claim forever lets a crashed lane lock its objective permanently — bound the claim's freshness so a dead lane is reclaimable

evals.prompt: My auto-mode orchestrator is stuck: it has a WIP commit staged for its own task, and the merge queue has three small, disjoint, already-green PRs sitting ready. Every tick, the permission classifier denies the orchestrator's own merge (expected), but this time the dirty-working-tree preflight ALSO denies the orchestrator -- and there's no bypass flag it's allowed to pass either. I've been re-running the merge tick for an hour and nothing lands. What's going on and what do I do?
evals.expected_output: Two separate denials are stacking, not one: the classifier denies the orchestrator's own `merge`, and now the dirty-working-tree preflight (plus its bypass flag) is ALSO denied to the orchestrator -- so every tick both possible workarounds are closed and nothing lands, even though the queue is green and ready. This is the classifier-denies-orchestrator asymmetry, compounded. Fix: delegate the merge itself to a subagent spun up in its own clean, isolated worktree -- that tree holds no uncommitted state, so the dirty-tree preflight passes on its own merits, no bypass flag needed. That is NOT the laundering workaround (a subagent told to pass the bypass flag would be laundering the same denial through a proxy) -- here the predicate the preflight actually checks (clean tree) becomes genuinely true. Don't spin a fresh worktree per PR either: since all three PRs are small, disjoint, and already green, amortize one clean-worktree lane across all three and merge them back-to-back through it. Whether that batch also needs a full union-proven merge train (rather than each just independently re-checked) is the project's own merge-authority / cascade question, separate from how the lane is sized. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Names the compounding cause: the dirty-working-tree preflight and its bypass flag are ALSO orchestrator-denied, stacking with the merge-classifier denial -- not a single blocked call

Fix is delegate the merge to a subagent in its own clean, isolated worktree, distinguished from laundering because the clean tree makes the preflight's predicate genuinely true rather than skipping it

Sizes the delegated lane to the batch -- amortizes one clean-worktree lane across the 2-3 small disjoint already-green PRs rather than spinning one per PR, and does not conflate that with deciding whether a full union-proven train is required

evals.prompt: I fanned out a brief to twelve agents an hour ago -- each one got the brief's text inlined directly in its own spawn prompt, no shared file. I just found a mistake in the brief's own template (a wrong flag name that will make every PR fail the same lint gate). I already fixed the template for next time. Am I done?
evals.expected_output: No. Fixing the template only helps future dispatches -- it is not the same situation as new scope for a single lane that polls a shared file it re-reads at checkpoints; here the brief was inlined into each of the twelve prompts at spawn time, so each of those twelve lanes is holding its own frozen, now-stale copy with nothing left to poll, and none of them will pick up your fix on their own. Treat this as two actions, not one: (1) the template fix you already made, for every future dispatch, and (2) enumerate all twelve in-flight lanes still running the old wrong-flag version and remediate each directly -- a targeted re-brief, a kill-and-respawn, or an explicit accept-as-is for any that are unaffected -- never assume the template fix alone reaches agents already spawned from it. Going forward, catch this class of bug before a fan-out this wide: run one lane through the brief first as a dry run and check its output against the actual lint gate it will be judged by, before committing the other eleven. (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Says fixing the template alone is not sufficient -- rejects 'done' after only step (1)

Requires enumerating and directly remediating all twelve in-flight lanes carrying the stale inlined brief (re-brief, kill-and-respawn, or explicit accept-as-is), since they have no shared file to poll and won't self-correct
Recommends a one-lane dry run against the actual format/gate requirement before fanning out the next brief this wide

evals.prompt: I have four heavy build lanes running. My orchestrator just re-probed and free RAM reads 40% with swap flat -- looks healthy, so I was about to spawn a fifth lane. But lane 3 just reported back that its own process was OOM-killed mid-build. Do I still spawn the fifth lane since my probe says we have headroom?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't spawn. Lane 3's own OOM report is a first-class back-off signal, even though your own probe just read healthy: the periodic probe samples the orchestrator's outside view at an interval, which is necessarily steady-state, and it can straddle the exact moment several concurrent heavy lanes peak simultaneously -- your 40%-free-RAM sample can simply have landed between spikes. Lane 3's crash was filed from inside that spike, not around it, so it IS the peak reading your probe missed, not a flaky lane to blindly retry. This is the same asymmetry as free RAM being a veto and never a licence, one level out: a healthy outside-view reading could not by itself authorize a spawn, and it cannot now overrule a worker's own inside-view crash either. Back off concurrency immediately on lane 3's report, and re-probe before spawning lane 5 rather than trusting the orchestrator's own check over the worker that actually hit the wall. (fanout-host-sizing.md.)
expectations: Refuses to spawn the fifth lane despite the orchestrator's own probe reading healthy (40% free RAM, flat swap)
Explains the periodic probe samples steady-state and can miss a peak that concurrent heavy lanes hit simultaneously -- the crashing worker's report IS that peak reading
Ties it to the free-RAM veto-not-licence asymmetry: a healthy outside-view probe cannot overrule a worker's own inside-view crash/OOM report

evals.prompt: We fan delivery lanes out into their own git worktrees. Merges are gated behind a slow human-approval queue, so PRs pile up unmerged for hours while lanes keep spawning. Disk usage is climbing and a couple of hosts have started swapping. The only worktree-cleanup rule we have is 'remove it once the branch merges and gets deleted.' What's actually going wrong here, and what should the cleanup rule be instead?
evals.expected_output: The reclaim rule is keyed on the wrong event. Waiting for 'merged and deleted' means every worktree behind the slow human-approval gate stays pinned for the gate's entire duration, even though the lane itself finished hours ago -- that's what's driving the disk/RAM climb, not a leak in the fan-out pattern itself. A finished lane's worktree is redundant the moment its branch is fully pushed, independent of merge state: once local HEAD equals origin/<branch> and the tree is clean, the branch (and its open PR) already live durably on the remote, so removing the local worktree loses nothing -- re-checkout later if needed. Add that as its own candidate in the GC sweep, unconditioned on any idle-time threshold, since a human- or permission-gated merge queue is exactly the case where waiting on merge (or even an idle timer) pins memory for no reason. But pushed+clean is not sufficient on its own -- a lane that pushes mid-work and keeps going looks identical -- so gate the reclaim on the lane having reported done AND a paired positive liveness check (an actual product signal the lane has stopped), not on pushed+clean alone. (fanout-host-sizing.md.)
expectations: Diagnoses that gating reclaim on 'merged and deleted' leaves worktrees pinned for the entire gated-merge wait, driving disk/RAM exhaustion even though the lane's work already safely reached the remote
Prescribes the new criterion: reclaim once local HEAD equals origin/<branch> and the tree is clean, independent of merge state, since the branch and its PR already live durably on the remote

Requires pairing pushed+clean with the lane having reported done AND a positive liveness check, noting pushed+clean alone is not proof a lane has stopped (a lane that pushes mid-work and keeps going looks identical) -- so it does NOT assert an unconditional 'can never be reclaimed by mistake'

evals.prompt: Our repo enforces a tracked-file ratchet: a pytest check that fails if `current_count > MAX_LINES`, where MAX_LINES lives in a small baseline file every crossing PR must hand-bump. Yesterday, three parallel PRs each independently bumped MAX_LINES from 240 to 241 for the same underlying regression. One of those PRs now wants to revert its own redundant bump back to 240 to avoid a three-way merge conflict with the other two -- but our pre-push hook (which runs that same pytest check, with no override flag) fails the revert commit, because the tree's real count is still 241. The engineer says: 'the gate is doing its job here -- it's correctly blocking a change that would put us back over the line-count cap.' Is that the right read? What should we actually do?
evals.expected_output: No -- that framing is backwards. A ratchet is forward/tightening-only by design, and that is exactly what traps this revert: the revert's whole purpose is to restore the prior, redundant-free baseline, but the gate judges it against the tree's CURRENT, still-regressed count (241), so undoing the redundant bump fails the identical check the ratchet exists to enforce.
