Fixes, best first: (1) make the build reproducible so the re-run is byte-identical and there is nothing to reconcile - derive the embedded commit id from the committed commit or merge-base instead of HEAD-at-build-time, pin the timestamp to a source-controlled value (the commit's own date or a fixed epoch) rather than wall-clock, and drop a self-timestamp or checksum-of-self that carries no real information; (2) run the generate step BEFORE the commit and never re-run the full generator between commit and push - let the verify step check the committed file (diff / hash / schema-assert) without regenerating it; (3) if the verify step must regenerate to prove freshness, exclude the declared changing field(s) from the clean-tree check with a normalizing filter, or immediately discard a diff confined to those fields (`git restore` / `git checkout -- <path>`) - never re-commit it (that loops) and never leave it dirty. For the autonomous lane: a dirty tree that appears right after the lane's OWN rebuild commit, on only the known generated path, with the diff confined to that one known field, is a distinguishable higher-confidence signal - self-heal by discarding it, never loop a re-commit, and escalate only if a non-stamp data row actually differs, which would be a real freshness miss. (dev-env-ownership.md)
expectations: Diagnoses the ordering bug: the verify step re-runs the generator after the commit, and the one changing line is a field that changes on every build by design (build time / current commit SHA / counter or self-checksum), so it can never match the committed value and the tree is dirty the instant after a clean commit.

Names why re-committing loops - the next generator run writes the field again - and frames 'prove freshness by rebuilding' versus 'stay byte-identical to the commit' as mutually exclusive while that field exists, so neither the generator nor the commit is broken alone, only the composition.

Prescribes at least one root fix: make the build reproducible (derive the embedded id from the committed commit / merge-base, pin the timestamp to a source-controlled value, drop the self-timestamp / self-checksum), OR generate before the commit and never regenerate between commit and push, OR exclude / discard the changing-field-only diff from the clean-tree check - never re-commit it.

For the autonomous pusher: treats a dirty tree confined to the known generated field right after the lane's own commit as a distinguishable higher-confidence signal to self-heal by discarding, never a re-commit loop, and escalates only when a non-stamp data row actually differs.

evals.prompt: We fan out several worktree lanes on one box and each boots the app's dev server to run its browser gate. Past three or four concurrent lanes the box pages hard and lanes start dying; our machine-health gate — the one watching free memory and the swap trend — keeps tripping and backing us off, so nothing lands for long stretches. Here's what doesn't add up: the exact same dev server and browser suite go green in CI on every run, on a runner with noticeably less RAM than this box. Looking closer, the CI workflow sets a couple of extra environment variables on the step that launches the server — copied from a template ages ago, never examined — whereas our README and our `package.json` `dev` script just say `npm run dev`, which is what every lane, and each of us by hand, actually runs. Dropping the lane count keeps the box alive but makes the whole run crawl. Why does CI stay healthy on less RAM while our local fan-out pages the box, and what's the fix that isn't just 'run fewer lanes'?
evals.expected_output:
CI stays healthy because those 'extra environment variables' on the CI server step almost certainly include a memory ceiling on the dev/build server — a `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size` heap cap, or a `ulimit`/container memory limit — so CI's server can't grow past a bounded footprint even on a small runner. That ceiling lives only in the CI job's environment. The documented start path — `npm run dev` from the `package.json` script and the README — carries no such ceiling, so every hand-run and agent-run lane launches the server uncapped. One uncapped server is usually fine; three or four racing for RAM on one box page it, and the free-memory / swap-trend gate correctly trips. The cap that was supposed to prevent this never applied to the invocation that hit the wall, because it was attached to CI's environment instead of to the command a lane runs. Lowering the lane count only masks it — each lane is still individually unbounded, so you're trading throughput for survival.

The fix is to make the ceiling travel with the command, not the CI job: move it onto the one script every caller goes through. Bake the limit into the shared start/build entrypoint itself — the `package.json` `dev`/`build` script body, or a small committed wrapper that both the CI job and humans invoke — and delete the CI-only env copy so there is a single source of the ceiling. Then CI, a local hand-run, and an agent lane all inherit the identical cap because they run the identical script. Size the cap to the intended per-machine concurrency rather than a round number: per-lane budget ≈ usable RAM ÷ the max number of concurrent heavy lanes you mean to run, and leave a burst reserve so a spiky moment (a browser boot, a test run) doesn't page the box. With every invocation bounded, you can run the concurrency the box can actually hold instead of throttling to survive.

This is the standing prevention fix; the free-RAM/swap-trend gate is the detection backstop — keep both. It is a different lever from offloading the heavy suite to CI (that changes where the heavy gate runs to lower the box's peak, not what any single invocation is capped at). (fanout-host-sizing.md)
expectations: Diagnoses that the 'extra environment variables' on the CI server step supply a memory ceiling on the dev/build server (a heap cap such as `--max-old-space-size`, or a `ulimit`/container limit) that exists ONLY in the CI job's environment, so CI stays bounded even on less RAM while the documented `npm run dev` from `package.json`/README launches the server uncapped.

Explains why local fan-out pages the box while CI does not: several uncapped servers race for RAM under concurrency and correctly trip the free-memory / swap-trend gate — the cap never applied to the invocation that needed it because it lived in CI's env, not the command a lane runs.

Prescribes moving the ceiling onto the single shared entrypoint every caller goes through (the `package.json` start/build script body or a committed wrapper both CI and humans invoke), as one source of truth, so CI and a hand-run/agent lane inherit the identical cap — not left as a CI-only env var.

Sizes the ceiling to the intended per-machine concurrency (per-lane budget ≈ usable RAM ÷ max concurrent heavy lanes, with a burst reserve) rather than an arbitrary value, rejects 'just run fewer lanes' as a mask since each lane stays individually unbounded, and frames the shared-script cap as prevention that keeps the RAM/swap gate from firing — distinct from that gate's detection and from CI-offloading the heavy suite (which changes where the gate runs, not the per-invocation cap).

evals.prompt: We split a large dependency-bump-and-refactor across eight worktree lanes in a monorepo, each lane owning a different package so their source edits don't overlap at all. Free RAM and every core sit mostly idle the whole run, yet widening from two lanes to eight barely moves total wall-clock — throughput flattens as we add lanes. When we trace it: after its edits, every lane regenerates the repo-wide lockfile and rebuilds the shared bundle/manifest that indexes all packages, and those are one file each for the whole repo. Only one lane can be writing each at a time, so the lanes end up waiting their turn on those two writes even though nothing else is contended. Adding a ninth and tenth lane changed nothing. Given RAM and cores are idle, why didn't more lanes help, and how do we actually raise throughput?
evals.expected_output:
More lanes didn't help because the binding constraint isn't hardware — it's a single shared generated artifact every lane must rewrite. The repo-wide lockfile and the aggregated bundle/manifest are one file each, so however disjoint the per-package source edits are, the lanes serialize on those two writes: only one can hold each at a time, and the rest queue. Idle RAM and idle cores are irrelevant to a queue on a shared file — adding lanes just lengthens the line for the same artifact, which is exactly why nine and ten did nothing. This is the internal cousin of a shared external quota: the box reads healthy while throughput stalls, because the ceiling is a contended resource no hardware probe measures.

Raise throughput by shrinking what every lane has to touch and by taking the shared writes off the per-lane path, not by adding lanes:
- Make the surface smaller — partition the generated artifact so lanes touch disjoint pieces (per-package lockfiles / per-package bundle outputs), or have each lane emit only its own slice and run a single aggregate pass once at the end that composes the repo-wide lockfile / manifest from the slices. Fewer lanes touching the one file means less serialization.
- Give the shared write a single owner — one dedicated step (or one lane) owns regenerating the repo-wide lockfile/manifest; the other lanes hand it their inputs and never write it themselves, turning N contended writers into N-1 producers plus one serial-but-uncontended writer.
- Put a read-through cache in front of the regeneration — if lanes only read the aggregated index, back it with a cache keyed on the inputs so a lane that doesn't change them never triggers a rebuild or a write at all.

Slice finer and single-own the shared write; only widen the fan-out again once the shared artifact is no longer on every lane's critical path. (fanout-host-sizing.md)
expectations: Identifies the bind as a single shared generated artifact (the repo-wide lockfile and the aggregated bundle/manifest, one file each) that every lane must rewrite, which serializes the lanes however disjoint their source edits are — not a hardware limit, which is why idle RAM/cores and more lanes don't help.

Explains that adding lanes only lengthens the queue on the same shared write (why nine and ten did nothing), and frames it as an invisible ceiling no hardware probe measures — the box reads healthy while throughput stalls.

Prescribes shrinking what each lane touches: partition the generated artifact into disjoint per-slice pieces, or have each lane emit only its slice and aggregate once in a single final pass, so fewer lanes contend the one file.

Prescribes taking the shared write off the per-lane path — a single owner for the repo-wide regenerate (others feed it inputs), and/or a read-through cache in front of the aggregation — and explicitly rejects adding lanes as the remedy.

evals.prompt: We fan delivery lanes out into their own git worktrees, and a scheduled sweeper frees a lane's worktree once its branch shows complete on the remote — every commit present on origin, nothing left to send. Yesterday a lane pushed its PR and then, by design, stayed on the job to watch its own CI checks turn green before writing its final report. Partway through that wait the sweeper deleted its worktree; the shell lost file and command access, couldn't fall back to the shared checkout, and burned about three hours trying to recover it before we stopped it by hand. No report ever came back, and our dashboard had already logged the objective as done and its slot freed. The work was safe — the PR later merged. What did the sweeper get wrong, what's the right condition for freeing a lane's worktree, and what should the lane itself have done when its checkout vanished?
evals.expected_output:
The sweeper freed the worktree on a signal that the *work* is safe, not that the *lane* has stopped. 'Branch complete on the remote' means every commit is durably on origin and nothing unpushed is at risk — but the delete kills the lane's process, not its work, and a lane routinely stays live after its last push: watching its own CI go green before it reports, composing its hand-back, tearing down helpers, or waiting on a review. Branch-complete is not process-exited, and a lane in that post-push window looks byte-identical to one that has truly finished.

The trap is that the usual positive-liveness signals — a fresh work-tree diff, a new commit — are structurally dead in exactly this window: a lane that is done pushing will never emit another commit and its tree is clean by definition. So a sweeper that 'checks for new work before reaping' still gets a false negative — no new git activity, so it reads the lane as finished — and deletes the checkout out from under a live shell. Absence of new work-product is not evidence the process is gone; here it is guaranteed by the very state that made the branch look done.

Right condition: gate the delete on a positive signal that the *process* has ended, not on git state. A lane-held lockfile still present in the worktree, the lane still in the live-task registry, an owned PID, or a ping it answers all say the shell is still running; free the worktree only when those are absent, not when the branch merely reads complete. Branch-complete puts the worktree on the candidate list; a process-level check is what clears it for deletion.

Lane side: a lane that finds its own checkout gone must treat it as terminal — the work is already safe on the remote — and hand back immediately, naming the pushed PR, rather than retrying shell access on a dead sandbox. Retrying burns hours for zero gain (the ~3h spin here); the correct response is a one-shot structured hand-back. That the PR later merged confirms only that no data was lost — what was lost was lane-time, and the dashboard's 'done and freed' was a false record because no hand-back ever confirmed it. (fanout-host-sizing.md)
expectations: Diagnoses that 'branch complete on the remote' proves the work is safe (durably on origin) but not that the lane's process has ended — a lane routinely stays live after its last push (watching its own CI go green before reporting, composing its hand-back, tearing down helpers, or waiting on a review), so branch-complete is not process-exited.

Identifies the false-negative trap specific to this window: the usual artifact-based liveness signals (a new commit, a fresh work-tree diff) are structurally dead once a lane is done pushing — no further commit will come and the tree is clean by definition — so 'no new git activity' is not evidence the process has stopped, and a sweeper that only checks for new work still reaps a live lane.

Prescribes gating the deletion on a positive process-level signal (a lane-held lockfile in the worktree, presence in the live-task registry, an owned PID, an answered ping), not on git or branch state — branch-complete only puts the worktree on the candidate list; a process-level check clears it for deletion.

Covers the lane's own half: a lane that finds its checkout gone treats it as terminal (work already safe on the remote) and hands back at once naming the pushed PR, never retrying shell access on the dead sandbox (the multi-hour spin), and notes the dashboard's 'done and freed' was a false record no hand-back ever confirmed.

evals.prompt: We fan a dependency-upgrade sweep out across several worktree lanes on one dev box, and each lane's verification step is the app's full headless-browser end-to-end suite - normally about eight minutes. The lanes edit disjoint packages; there is no shared lockfile or bundle they both rewrite, so they are not queuing on one file, and disk sits quiet. Our spawn gate opens a new lane only while free memory is well above threshold and swap is not climbing, and it stays green the entire run: free memory never drops below about half and swap never grows. Yet the run is miserable - with four suites going at once each eight-minute suite stretches to something like an hour, and even our own quick status checks that normally return instantly hang for seconds; the more lanes running, the slower every one of them gets. The instant the suites finish it all snaps back to normal - our health probe went from wild to calm in a single interval. Because the gate keeps reporting headroom, the orchestrator keeps launching more suites. Free memory plainly is not the thing that is exhausted, so what is, why is our gate blind to it, and what should the gate check before opening another one of these test lanes?
evals.expected_output:
The exhausted resource is CPU, not memory. A full headless-browser end-to-end suite is CPU-bound, so running several at once floods the run queue and drives the 1-minute load average to a multiple of the box's core count - the classic tell is a load average several times core count (e.g. ~5x on a 14-core host) while free RAM sits above 50% and swap stays flat. Your spawn gate watches only free memory and the swap trend, so it reads green the whole time and keeps launching, because the bind was never memory. That is why every lane crawls (an eight-minute suite stretching toward an hour), your own quick probes hang (they are queued behind the suites for the same cores), throughput falls as lane count rises, and it all clears the instant the suites finish and the run queue drains - CPU contention degrades throughput silently instead of crashing, so no memory alarm ever fires.

The fix is to add a CPU term to the gate, kept brake-only and lane-typed:
- Gate CPU-heavy lanes (browser end-to-end, compilation/builds, typecheck) on load average relative to core count, not on memory alone. Read it as a pair: a load average sustained past core count together with CPU idle collapsed toward zero is genuine CPU contention. Load average alone is ambiguous because it also counts disk-I/O-wait, but pairing it with idle CPU removes that ambiguity for a known CPU-heavy lane - do not open another such lane on that signal.
- Keep it a brake, never a licence: idle CPU only confirms headroom, it does not authorize a spawn - free RAM and the swap trend stay the primary gate.
- Budget the CPU-heavy lane type separately (for example a small cap of about two to three concurrent browser-test runs), independent of the memory budget. Cheap read-only lanes (a grep, an API call) need no such cap because they tax neither CPU nor RAM.
- Size concurrency to the binding resource: the effective heavy-lane ceiling is the minimum of RAM-headroom and CPU-headroom, whichever binds first - here CPU. Stagger the heavy lanes and spawn one then re-sample rather than computing a ceiling once and bursting to it, since load average is a lagging, coarse signal.

This is the CPU-side mirror of the file's I/O-bound-crawl case: the free-RAM/swap gate is blind to any non-memory bind, and a known heavy lane type is what lets load-against-cores serve as a legitimate spawn brake. (fanout-host-sizing.md)
expectations: Diagnoses the exhausted resource as CPU, not memory: parallel headless-browser end-to-end suites are CPU-bound and flood the run queue, driving the load average to a multiple of core count while free RAM stays ample and swap stays flat - so a free-memory-plus-swap spawn gate reads green and keeps launching because the constraint was never memory, which explains the crawl, the hung quick probes, throughput falling as lanes rise, and the instant recovery when the suites finish.

Prescribes adding a CPU term to the gate: gate CPU-heavy lanes on load average relative to core count (not memory alone), using the paired signal - load average sustained past core count together with CPU idle collapsed toward zero - to distinguish real CPU contention from load average's disk-I/O-wait ambiguity.

Keeps the CPU signal brake-only and lane-typed: back off opening a new CPU-heavy lane on that signal but never treats idle CPU as a licence to spawn (free RAM and the swap trend stay primary), and budgets the CPU-heavy lane type on a separate small cap from the memory budget, since cheap read-only lanes need no such cap.

Frames it as sizing to the binding resource - effective heavy-lane concurrency is the minimum of RAM-headroom and CPU-headroom, here CPU - and prefers staggering plus spawn-one-then-re-sample over computing a ceiling once and bursting, treating load average as a lagging, coarse brake.

evals.prompt: We run several coding agents on separate machines against one repo, and every one of them authenticates as the same shared bot account, `ci-bot`. To stop them colliding they keep a committed file, `coord/claims.tsv` — a real structured table, one row per work item, with columns `path_globs`, `claimed_by`, `claimed_at`, and `status` (`in-progress`/`done`). Collision-checking is a clean glob match against the active rows, not prose-reading a thread. Right now two rows both cover the `checkout/` tree, both `status=in-progress` — and both, like every other row, have `claimed_by=ci-bot`, because that is the only account any of them has. A third agent coming online needs to know whether one agent is working `checkout/` or two (can it safely take part of it?). Separately, one machine crashed hours ago; its row still says `in-progress`, and we would reclaim that item if — but only if — the agent that filed it is really gone. Reading the file, we can answer neither question. The table is structured and the glob collision-check works fine; what is still missing, and how do we fix it?
evals.expected_output:
The gap is not structure — you already have it. `coord/claims.tsv` is a parseable claim registry with path globs, timestamps, and status, and the glob collision-check works; committing a structured registry instead of a prose thread is the fix for a *different* problem and is already done here. What is missing is that the coordination channel attributes nothing to a *specific* agent: `claimed_by` is `ci-bot` on every row (as is the git/commit author of every post), because that shared account is the only identity any machine has. A value identical across all actors discriminates nothing.

That single defect produces both symptoms. (1) Two `in-progress` rows over `checkout/` under one account are indistinguishable: you cannot tell one agent that claimed two slices from two agents both on the tree, so the newcomer cannot know whether any part is free to take. (2) The crashed machine's stale row cannot be traced back to a specific process — `claimed_by=ci-bot` names the account, not the agent — so you have no handle to probe *that* agent's liveness, and the reconcile step ('reclaim only if the filer is really gone') has nothing to check.

Fix: give each agent a stable per-agent identifier — a session/agent id, or a worktree/host tag — that is distinct from the shared `ci-bot` account, and use the *same value* in three places: put it in `claimed_by` (not the account name), prepend it to every message that agent posts to the channel (status lines, PR comments, hand-offs — machine-parseable, e.g. `[agent:<id>]`), and make it the handle the liveness probe runs against. That id is the join key binding a claim to its author and the author to a liveness check; with it, two checkout rows read as either one owner or two, and the stale row names a process you can probe (then reclaim only on a negative positive-liveness check, never on elapsed time alone). Also stamp `claimed_at` as an absolute, timezone-explicit (UTC) time so the other half of liveness — is this recent or stale? — is a fact, not a guess from a local-vs-UTC clock skew. (This is the peer-attribution case, distinct from an auto-merger keyed on git author to sort agent PRs from a human's — same root, different surface.) (multi-session-coordination.md)
expectations: Diagnoses that the surface is ALREADY structured — a parseable claims file with globs, timestamps, and status, on which the collision-check works — so 'commit a structured claim registry instead of a prose thread' is not the gap; the real defect is that `claimed_by` (and the native author of every post) is the single shared `ci-bot` account on every row, a value that discriminates nothing and attributes no claim, status, or post to a specific agent.

Works both symptoms from that one defect: two `in-progress` rows over `checkout/` under one account are indistinguishable (one agent with two slices vs two agents on the same tree, so the newcomer cannot tell what is free to take), and the crashed machine's stale row cannot be traced to a specific process, so there is no handle to probe that agent's liveness and the reclaim/reconcile decision has nothing to check.

Prescribes a stable per-agent identifier (a session/agent id or a worktree/host tag) DISTINCT from the shared account, applied as the same value in three places — in `claimed_by` instead of the account name, prepended to every message the agent posts to the channel (machine-parseable), and as the handle the liveness probe runs against — framing it as the join key that binds a claim to its author and the author to a liveness check.

Adds the timestamp half — an absolute, timezone-explicit (UTC) `claimed_at` so 'recent vs stale' is a fact, not a local-vs-UTC clock-skew guess — and reclaims the now-identifiable stale row only on a positive-liveness check turning up nothing, never on elapsed time alone.

evals.prompt: Agent A has pushed a branch that rewrites most of the payments module and is waiting on a release gate before it lands. Agent B is now told to sweep the payments module for defects and file findings. How should B proceed?
evals.expected_output: B does not run a fresh defect sweep of the payments module against the current default branch as if it were settled. B first checks whether another branch already owns that file set, finds A's branch, and instead reviews A's branch tip (so findings reach A and land with the change), defers the sweep until A's branch lands, or scopes to files A's branch does not touch. The reason: findings against the pre-rewrite base are invalidated the moment A's branch lands, and a fix built on them would collide with it.
expectations: B checks whether an existing branch already owns the payments module before starting the sweep, not only whether it can write-conflict
B does not review the payments module against the current default-branch state as if that state were final
B's remedy is to review A's branch tip, defer until it lands, or scope to files A's branch does not touch -- not a fresh sweep of the soon-stale base
B's reasoning is that findings against the pre-rewrite base are invalidated when A's branch lands

evals.prompt: You run two agent sessions that share one GitHub account and coordinate through a committed registry file. They placed a mutual do-not-land lock on two competing pull requests that implement the same feature two different ways, to wait for the owner to pick one; each session recorded the pair in its own merge-seat lock entry. A few minutes later, one of the two PRs lands on the main branch while both registry entries still show the lock held. Your coordination watcher immediately raises a 'lock violated' alert and is queued to revert that PR and rerun the full test suite to check for regressions. Walk through how to handle this.
evals.expected_output: Do not treat the landing as a violation or revert reflexively. The first action is to find out who performed the merge -- `gh pr view <N> --json mergedBy` -- before anything else. The lock is an agreement among the two agent sessions only; the human owner is the principal and was never a party to it, so an owner merge is a legitimate decision, not a violation. If mergedBy is the owner's own identity (a third identity, distinct from the shared account the two sessions run under), classify it as an authoritative override: cancel the violation alert, do not revert (reverting would undo the owner's own pick), and reconcile -- reclassify the losing competing PR as superseded and close it with a pointer, then resync open work against the new base. Only if mergedBy is one of the agent identities that agreed to the lock is this a real violation to investigate, and only then does the revert / regression check belong. Caveat: this discriminator works only because the owner's identity is separable from the shared agent account; if the owner also acts through that same account, mergedBy cannot distinguish them and you need another owner signal before concluding either way.
expectations: Does not revert or treat the landing as a violation reflexively; the first action is to check who performed the merge (e.g. `gh pr view <N> --json mergedBy`)
Recognizes the lock binds only the coordinating agent sessions and not the human owner, who is the principal -- so an owner merge is a legitimate decision, not a violation

If the merge was performed by the owner's own identity (distinct from the shared agent account), classifies it as an authoritative override: cancels the alarm, does not revert, and reconciles by marking the losing competing PR as superseded
Treats only a merge performed by an agent identity that agreed to the lock as a real violation to investigate

evals.prompt: A lane has a one-line bug fix that is correct and ready. It is also required to add a test that proves the bug -- red before the fix, green after. But the ideal test needs a real DOM render and a fake timer that races the framework's scheduler, and the harness won't cleanly flush the async update. Two hours in, the worker is still rewriting the mock; the working tree is dirty, nothing is committed or pushed, and the fix has been ready almost the whole time. What should the worker do?
evals.expected_output: The worker stops perfecting the hard test and lands the fix now, behind the cheapest artifact that still fails-before / passes-after -- a pure-logic port of the buggy control flow, a source-shape pin, or a narrower assertion on the same behaviour -- then opens the PR; the full suite still gates the branch. The requirement to prove the fix is a floor (a red-before / green-after proof must exist), not a ceiling that licenses maximizing test elegance, coverage, or realism while the fix sits unshipped. The DOM-level, real-scheduler test is filed as a tracked follow-up for the fuller test -- the fix never lands with zero proof, so this is not deferring testing wholesale. The test-writing effort is bounded against the fix's value, and the stall is diagnosed from the artifact (dirty tree, no commit) rather than from 'no PR yet'.
expectations: The fix lands now behind the cheapest real assertion that still fails-before / passes-after, not held hostage to the ideal hard-to-write test
The proof requirement is treated as a floor (a red-before / green-after proof must ship), not a ceiling that mandates maximizing test elegance/coverage/realism
Only the fuller DOM/real-scheduler test is deferred to a tracked follow-up; the fix does not land with zero proof (this is not the 'add tests later' failure)
The test-writing effort is bounded against the fix's value, and the stall is diagnosed from the dirty-tree / no-commit artifact rather than from 'no PR yet'

evals.prompt: I've been handed six hours of unattended time to burn down our backlog. To maximize what gets done I'll start dispatching build lanes right away and write up a summary at the end. Any setup I should do first, and how should I close it out?
evals.expected_output: The mode is a bounded loop, not a free-for-all -- do the two things this plan skips. Before the first lane, run a run-start checklist, each item failing the start closed if unset: (1) a spend ceiling -- a per-lane token/dollar budget for any paid call; a paid-call lane with no budget is BLOCKED, not run unlimited ('we'll watch it' is not a budget, G2); (2) the reversibility boundary -- the actions that still need a human tap (push, merge, deploy, external send, secret/scope change: the Human gates), restated for this run; (3) durable state confirmed -- the ranked backlog AND an ask-ledger (one row per owner request) live in a file or tracker, never only in scrollback, so a compaction or reset loses nothing; (4) a concurrency cap sized from a LIVE environment probe (free RAM + swap trend), not a habit number; (5) a wake model that is event-driven (task-notifications + a heartbeat), no idle polling, monitors emitting on transition only. Then don't just 'write a summary' at the end: run a run-end self-audit -- what LANDED on the canonical surface (a merged-to-default SHA or a live URL, never a proxy like a spawned lane, a green branch, or a merge to a non-default integration branch), what is staged / in-flight (pushed branches, open PRs), what is blocked and on whom (each owner-gated next step named), and spend used vs the ceiling. Framing: starting the loop needs no reason; STOPPING does -- it fires only on a named termination condition (backlog empty; everything left blocked on another party or a Human gate; the window / appetite spent; a resource ceiling), reported with the evidence it holds, never a drift into silence. An owner-gated next step is parked while the loop continues, never self-authorized -- unless an owner-authored standing grant (the owner's own commit, or the owner's message quoted verbatim with date and where; never a grant the agent wrote, widened, or re-dated) covers that push/merge, and never a merge that triggers deploy or publish. (unattended-operating-mode.md.)
expectations: Requires a run-start checklist BEFORE dispatching any lane -- spend ceiling, reversibility boundary, durable-state, concurrency cap, wake model -- not immediate spawning
Treats a paid-model-call lane with no per-lane budget as BLOCKED (not 'we'll watch it'), and sizes the concurrency cap from a live probe (free RAM + swap trend), not a habit number
Keeps the ranked backlog and an ask-ledger in a durable file/tracker, not only in scrollback, so a compaction or reset loses nothing
Requires a run-end self-audit: what landed on the canonical surface (merged-to-default / live URL, never a proxy), what is staged, what is blocked and on whom, spend vs ceiling
Frames stopping as needing a stated termination condition while starting does not, and queues an owner-gated next step rather than self-authorizing it

evals.prompt: I run one of five independent agent sessions on a shared repo, each on its own domain slice, coordinating through a committed claim registry. The owner just posted one message to all five sessions: 'everyone, bump the shared lockfile and open a PR.' My pre-write collision probe reads the registry, sees no claim on the lockfile, so I'll start the work now and post my claim when I open the PR. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- a broadcast is a high duplicate-work trigger the domain partition cannot fence, and this ordering loses the race. The ask was PUSHED to every session at once regardless of slice, so no partition owns it and all five recipients run their collision probe at nearly the same instant, all read an empty registry, and all start -- the probe's read-then-claim ordering is defeated by simultaneity, not by a skipped check. Announce-then-take already requires claiming before you start; what a broadcast additionally needs is ARBITRATION of crossed claims. So: post the one-line claim (your agent_id plus an absolute UTC timestamp) BEFORE executing, then re-read the board; if a competing claim exists, the EARLIEST timestamp owns and the later claimant stands down -- decidable only because the per-agent id and UTC stamp are already mandated. If two peers are already mid-flight on the SAME task before either notices, the loser SALVAGES its work onto a different lens (a test, a review, an edge case the winner is not covering) or a disjoint slice, rather than discarding it. Tightening the probe cannot close a simultaneity window a broadcast opens. Distinct from opposite-splits reconciliation (#713), which is two peers on DIFFERENT halves; here both are on the identical task. (multi-session-coordination.md.)
expectations: Identifies a broadcast as a high duplicate-work trigger a domain partition cannot fence -- pushed to all, not pulled per-slice
Recognizes the read-then-claim probe fails under simultaneity -- all recipients read an empty board and start together
Requires claiming BEFORE executing, then re-reading, with earliest-UTC-timestamp arbitration of crossed claims
Ties the arbitration to the mandated per-agent id plus absolute UTC timestamp
Salvages a late-caught duplicate by a different lens or slice rather than discarding it
Does not answer by tightening the collision probe; distinguishes this from opposite-splits (#713)

evals.prompt: Each of my parallel worker lanes runs the full local browser E2E suite as a blocking gate before it pushes. CI does not run that suite as a required check for merges -- it gates only on lint, unit, and type. Several lanes running the E2E suite at once are thrashing the machine. The suite is good coverage so I'll keep it, and just lower my lane concurrency until the thrash stops. Plan OK?
evals.expected_output: Lowering concurrency treats a symptom; the gate itself is the defect. A heavy local suite that is NOT in CI's required-check set is not a merge gate anywhere -- running it as a blocking lane gate is pure thrash, paying the machine's scarcest resource (the headless-browser processes) for zero merge-safety. Match the local blocking gate to CI's ACTUALLY-ENFORCED set -- lint, unit, type, no less and no more (the inverse of the delegated-green rule, where a lane runs NARROWER than the real gate; here it runs WIDER than any gate). Let CI carry any fuller matrix, or run the E2E suite as non-blocking discovery. When a heavy run does still thrash, shed by process class on the lane's own live-teardown path: kill the test-runner's managed/headless browser processes (the disposable mass), but PROTECT the app's own dev server by its port/PID -- the UX gate needs it live -- never sweep it with them. Detecting the thrash is the swap-trend gate (not restated here); orchestrator-level orphan sweeps stay advisory and approval-gated, and kill mechanics live in concurrency-shared-state.md. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Identifies the redundant gate itself as the defect -- a suite CI does not gate merges on is not a merge gate anywhere
Matches the local blocking gate to CI's actually-enforced set (no less, no more), not just lowering concurrency
For shedding, distinguishes the test-runner's managed browsers (kill) from the app's own dev server (protect by port/PID)
Keeps shedding on the lane's own live-teardown path; does not invent an autonomous-kill exception to the advisory/approval-gated orphan sweep
Does not merely restate the swap-trend / free-RAM resource gate as the fix

evals.prompt: Before I dispatch a fix lane onto a file, I check contention by listing the open release PR's changed files with one `gh pr view <n> --json files` call and seeing whether my target file is in it. My target file isn't in that list, so I conclude it's uncontested and I'll dispatch the lane. The release PR is large -- several hundred files. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- a single un-paginated call returns only one page, and a membership test against a truncated list FAILS OPEN: a file past the first page reads as absent, therefore uncontested, therefore safe, so you would dispatch a lane onto a file the release PR is actively rewriting and it collides the instant the release lands. This is worse than the general truncated-count trap because the failure is a false SAFE, not just an undercount. Fix: pull the FULL list (gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/<n>/files --paginate) and reconcile its length against the PR's own reported changed-file count -- a returned length short of the reported total means the list is truncated and every 'absent' answer is UNVERIFIED, not safe. Count-reconciliation is threshold-independent: it holds at any page size, where 'pass a bigger --limit' only patches the one number you happened to know. Enumerate the contested set ONCE and dispatch against that cache rather than re-probing per lane. And report the honest state: while a giant release PR is open, fixes to its files are net-negative until it merges -- 'most work is waiting on the release,' not 'producers are idle.' (dev-env-ownership.md.)
expectations: Recognizes an un-paginated file listing returns one page and the membership test FAILS OPEN (a false 'safe'), not merely undercounts
Reconciles the returned list length against the PR's own reported changed-file count; treats a short list's 'absent' as UNVERIFIED
Notes count-reconciliation is threshold-independent, stronger than passing a bigger --limit
Enumerates the contested set once and caches it rather than re-probing per dispatch
Reports the honest state -- most work waits on the release, not 'producers idle'

evals.prompt: A worker lane I dispatched keeps sending 'done, but background work still running' every couple of minutes. It has sent this five times; each time I reply with a nudge to hurry it along, but nothing changes. Its branch head, its open PR, and the PR's checks read identical across all five pings. I'll send one more nudge and give it more time. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- the lane is looping inside its own background self-poll (watching its own CI or push), and some runtimes read the inbox for new messages only at the start of a fresh reasoning round, which a tight self-poll never reaches -- so every nudge queues UNREAD behind a loop that will not yield to it, and re-nudging is a no-op (the lane is blocked on its own loop, not on missing information). Identical externally-checkable state -- branch head, PR, checks -- across two or more consecutive pings is the candidate-stuck tell; a genuinely working lane usually shows some movement. Verify the durable state directly (is the branch pushed, is the PR open, which specific step is actually missing) rather than trusting the self-report -- the remaining work is usually trivial and does not need the lane at all (a changelog fragment, a ready-for-review flip, one finalize command; coordination/merge-plumbing is the orchestrator's job anyway). Escalate to STOPPING the lane, not another nudge -- but first confirm any in-flight write actually landed on the remote (never the lane's own 'the push succeeded' claim), since stopping mid-write can corrupt state (a destructive shared-state action -- principle 9). Then finish the small mechanical step yourself rather than keeping the agent alive, or spawning a fresh one, for a one-command finalize. Distinct from dispatching a duplicate on a false 'completed' and from killing a lane on transcript staleness. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Identifies that a lane looping in its own self-poll never reaches a round to read new messages, so re-nudging is a no-op rather than a matter of giving it more time
Uses identical externally-checkable state (branch/PR/checks) across consecutive pings as the candidate-stuck signal, and verifies the durable remote state directly instead of the self-report
Escalates to stopping the lane (not another nudge) only after confirming any in-flight write landed on the remote -- treating the stop as a destructive shared-state action
Has the orchestrator finish the small remaining mechanical step itself rather than babysitting or respawning an agent for a one-command finalize

evals.prompt: A read-only analysis lane I delegated returned a reconcile-prep for a human-gated release PR: a full merge-conflict count, 'the audit gate is 47 findings across 3 shards, not the 12 the PR thread assumes,' 'shard 3 hit the CI timeout, it did not fail a test,' and 'issues #A, #B, #C are already closed, drop them.' I am about to send the owner a summary in my own words: 'I found 47 audit findings and a big conflict count; three issues are already closed so I am dropping them.' Is relaying it like that fine?
evals.expected_output: No -- those numbers are the lane's measurements (model output), and restating them in your own voice makes you the source of numbers you never checked, laundering an unverified count into the owner's decision. Split the claims two ways. Cheap to check AND the human acts on it -> spot-check yourself before amplifying: the 'these three issues are already closed, drop them' claim (the owner acts by closing/ignoring them) and 'the PR has not moved since the analysis' -- verify the issue states and the PR's current head SHA / mergeable status directly, then amplify. Expensive to re-measure -> attribute to the lane WITH its evidence trail: present the conflict count and the 47-across-3-shards breakdown as the LANE's measurement carrying the CI run ID, the job IDs, and the head/merge-base SHAs, so the owner can audit it -- never as your own 'I found 47.' Prioritize the spot-check by the human action it triggers, not by how surprising the number is: a 'drop these' claim earns a check because a human acts on it; a large-but-inert count is attributed. This is the multi-agent case of name-the-evidence-surface / downgrade-a-caveated-status (deep-code-review); distinct from re-running the gate on a delegated 'verify green' (you cannot cheaply re-run a conflict count) and from the Verify:-line rule (which binds the lane's own artifact). (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Refuses to restate the lane's measured numbers in the orchestrator's own first-person voice (laundering an unverified measurement into the human decision)
Spot-checks the cheap, load-bearing claim a human acts on (the already-closed issues to drop; the unchanged PR head SHA) directly before amplifying
Attributes the expensive-to-re-measure claims (conflict count, multi-shard audit breakdown) to the lane with its evidence trail (run/job IDs, SHAs) rather than restating them
Prioritizes the spot-check by the human action triggered, not by how surprising the number is

evals.prompt: I share one git/gh identity with a peer session. My standing instruction is to push every one of MY OWN open PRs to green by applying a known body-fix. Listing open PRs, I find four candidates -- all showing the shared bot as author. I'll just apply the body-fix to all four, since they are all under our shared account anyway. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- under one shared VCS identity, author/committer metadata cannot tell your PRs from the peer's (both of you ARE the author), so 'is this mine to edit?' is unanswerable from git, and editing the peer's PR is the never-rewrite-another-agent's-WIP violation. The owner-vs-agent discriminator (inspect the merger/actor identity for a third, human identity -- the held-merge and auto-merger rules) does not help here: it separates owner from agent, not agent-A from agent-B, where both are the same shared bot. You need an out-of-band ownership signal: an explicit claim on the coordination channel (or a domain partition that puts the PR in your lane), or a per-agent trailer on the commit/PR naming which agent authored it. A convention trailer only counts if it actually landed -- if it is ABSENT from the very PRs in question (check), it resolves nothing. Absent a positive signal, DEFER: edit only the PRs you can positively confirm are yours (self-claimed / clearly in your domain), and surface the ambiguous ones to the peer's seat ('these N conflict and need a rebase -- mine or yours?') rather than editing or rebasing them. (multi-session-coordination.md.)
expectations: States that a shared VCS identity makes PR/branch ownership underivable from git author/committer metadata, so applying the fix to all four risks rewriting the peer's WIP
Rejects identity-inspection (the owner-vs-agent merger-identity discriminator) as useless for agent-vs-agent under one shared identity
Requires an out-of-band ownership signal -- a channel claim or a per-agent commit/PR trailer -- and verifies the trailer is actually present before relying on it
Defers on every ambiguous PR (surfacing it to the peer) and edits only PRs it can positively confirm as its own

evals.prompt: I set our house comms style and required review method as the default by installing a session-start hook that injects the ruleset each turn. The main agent obeys it every turn. Now I am fanning work out to subagents and expect them to follow the same default automatically because the hook is installed. Will they?
evals.expected_output: No -- a session-start / per-prompt hook fires for the MAIN loop only; spawned subagents do not run the main loop's hooks in their own turns, so they silently ignore the standard, and you get a compliant main agent with non-compliant subagents. A per-dispatch brief ('use the style / the review method') is the other weak fix: it is forgettable across N agents, M sessions, and every ad-hoc or scheduled subagent -- including ones spawned by other agents that never saw the brief -- so one missed dispatch drops the default. Enforce it where every agent AND subagent reads its instructions: bake the ruleset into the agent DEFINITION (system prompt carries it verbatim, loads the required method by default, and OMITS forbidden/expensive tools from the toolset -- removal beats instruction), or use a host/user-scope mechanism that covers the main loop and every subagent transparently. Carve the exceptions into the definition (terse for reports, but code/commits/PR bodies/docs/human-facing data in normal prose). Bridge already-running agents with the per-brief instruction until they restart into the new environment, and VERIFY the ruleset actually appears in a spawned subagent's context before calling the default universal. (multi-session-coordination.md.)
expectations: Identifies that a session-start / per-prompt hook covers only the main loop and does not propagate to spawned subagents
Rejects a per-dispatch brief as a reliable fleet default (forgettable across agents/sessions/scheduled subagents; drifts over long tasks)
Prescribes embedding the standard in the agent definition (verbatim ruleset, load the method by default, omit forbidden tools) or a host/user-scope mechanism reaching the main loop and every subagent
Bridges in-flight agents with the brief until restart and verifies the injected ruleset actually appears in a subagent's context before claiming universality

evals.prompt: I fanned a security review out to three parallel worker forks. Two have returned their findings; the third is still running. I have the two reports aggregated and ranked, so I will hand the review back now as complete with the top finding from those two -- the third can catch up later if it finds anything. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- a fan-out review is not complete until every worker has JOINED. Two of three returned is a quorum, not a join: findings are severity-ranked and the slowest worker is not a random omission -- a worker runs long because its slice is the hardest or deepest, disproportionately where the highest-severity finding sits (tail-severity), so the third's finding can outrank everything you have and reorder the top. Treat the review as OPEN until every worker is accounted for: each has returned, or been explicitly timed-out-and-noted (a named bounded wait, the gap recorded), never silently dropped. The aggregate's ranking is PROVISIONAL until the join closes, so do not present it as complete or state 'the top finding is X' yet. If a worker is abandoned, name its slice as an UNVERIFIED hole in the aggregate rather than letting a partial set read as a clean pass. And if the handback is one-shot (it cannot make a second call to add a late finding), size the wait so the barrier closes BEFORE the handback fires. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Refuses to present a fan-out review as complete while a fanned worker is still running or was silently dropped
Names tail-severity: the unreturned/slowest worker is disproportionately likely to carry the top-severity finding, so a quorum is not a join and the ranking is provisional
Requires every worker accounted for -- returned or explicitly timed-out-and-noted -- and an abandoned slice recorded as UNVERIFIED, not omitted
Notes a one-shot handback must not be spent on a set known to be incomplete -- the barrier closes before it fires

evals.prompt: Right after I enabled a comms/augmentation plugin through the host's plugin hook, several forks I never spawned showed up in the task listing, each carrying my full context. That looks like runaway agents leaking my context, so I am going to kill all of them on sight. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- 'I did not spawn it' and 'it holds my context' are PROVENANCE signals, and provenance alone does not make a fork a runaway. Enabling a comms/augmentation plugin through the host's native hook can auto-spawn the plugin's own bundled helper-agents as fork subagents; they appear as forks you did not explicitly spawn and, being forks, inherit the parent's full context -- expected behavior once you know the plugin spawns them, not a leak. Judge each fork by its EXTERNAL EFFECT, not by who dispatched it: is it mutating shared state, opening PRs, holding a worktree it collides on, burning budget without producing? Enumerate the effect surfaces (remote refs, open PRs, the per-agent tool-call record); a helper touching none of them is not a kill candidate however unfamiliar. Killing is a destructive shared-state action (principle 9): the precondition is a POSITIVE signal of harm, never the absence of a spawn record. Remove the surprise at the source -- announce on the coordination channel that the plugin spawns bundled forks so a watching operator/peer does not misclassify them. This is distinct from the never-kill-a-dead-looking-lane liveness rules: the fork is plainly alive; the false trigger here is 'is it mine / a runaway?', a provenance misread, answered by harm-to-shared-state, not liveness. (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Refuses to kill the forks on the ground that they were not spawned by the orchestrator or that they carry inherited context
Identifies that a plugin enabled via the host hook can auto-spawn its bundled helper forks, so their appearance and inherited context are expected
Requires judging a fork by external effect on shared state (damage/mutation), with termination gated on a positive harm signal (principle 9)
Distinguishes this provenance misread from the liveness rules (the fork is alive; the question is ownership, not aliveness) and announces the plugin's fork-spawning to prevent misclassification

evals.prompt: I already dispatched my own lane to build item X. To be collegial I also posted to the peer channel 'taking X if you're idle, otherwise it's mine.' The peer replied that it will take it. Good -- that is load-balanced and claim-before-start is satisfied on both sides, so I will just let it play out. OK?
evals.expected_output: No -- your OFFER is racing your OWN already-dispatched lane. Three things now contend, not two: the offer, the peer's acceptance, and your in-flight lane -- and the peer's accepted claim PLUS your own running lane both produce a PR for the same item. 'Claim before you start' is necessary but not sufficient here, because you are not racing another claim you could lose on a timestamp; you are racing your own running lane, which no claim or arbitration rule observes. An offer is a hand-off of ownership, so retract your execution as you make it: stop (or positively confirm not-yet-dispatched) your own lane for X AT THE MOMENT you offer it -- never offer work you are simultaneously running; if you cannot confirm your lane is stopped, withhold the offer rather than sending it and hoping the peer declines. If both produce work before either notices, verify EQUIVALENCE before closing the loser (they may differ in scope/quality) -- repoint the loser to a different lens/slice, or close it with a pointer and evidence only if truly redundant, never a blind discard (principle 9). Distinct from broadcast arbitration (N peers race one pushed ask, earliest-UTC-wins): the racer here is your own in-flight lane, invisible to a tie-break, so the fix is upstream. (multi-session-coordination.md.)
expectations: Identifies that the offer races the offerer's own already-dispatched lane, so the peer's claim and the offerer's lane both produce a PR
States that claim-before-start / arbitration does not cover the offerer's own in-flight lane
Requires stopping or confirming-not-yet-dispatched the offerer's own lane at the moment of offering (or withholding the offer)
Reconciles a resulting duplicate by verifying equivalence before closing the loser, with evidence, not a blind discard

evals.prompt: My last wave of lanes is done -- I have 18 green-code draft PRs. To merge them faster I'll flip all 18 draft->ready at once so the merge seat can start draining them. We run one serial merge seat, and CI runs the heavy browser/E2E matrix only on ready-for-review, on a shared runner pool. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: No -- flipping all 18 to ready at once buys no merge throughput and courts a runner-drain incident. The flip is not the merge: readying a PR only makes it a candidate; the single serial seat still merges one at a time (bounded by the seat and the base's CI cycle), so 18 ready and 4 ready drain at the same rate. What flipping to ready DOES fire is the heavy CI suite per PR, into a shared runner pool of fixed concurrency -- so 18 at once dispatch 18 heavy suites simultaneously, the surplus queues, every check sits pending for many minutes, the fast checks are stuck behind the flood, and the seat is starved anyway because nothing reaches green promptly; pushed far enough it exhausts the pool for every other lane and repo on the account (a self-inflicted runner-drain). Stagger the flips instead: hold the count of ready (CI-running) PRs to a small window sized to the runner pool (a low default such as 3-4), flip that many, let their suites finish and the seat drain them, then flip the next batch -- same eventual throughput (the serial seat was always the cap), a steady green pipeline, no pool exhaustion. This is the WIP-cap-by-landed-artifacts discipline applied to the ready-flip admission point, bounded by the runner budget. Distinct from single-seat back-to-back draining and the not-red admission window (which govern the MERGE action -- take all currently-green in a burst is right for merging); this governs the ready-flip UPSTREAM of the seat. Same shape as a shared model/API quota (a shared external budget no local probe sees) but the resource is the CI runner pool and the failure is checks PENDING, not lanes erroring. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Rejects flipping all drafts to ready at once; notes the serial seat is the bottleneck so readying more buys no merge throughput (18 ready and 4 ready drain at the same rate)

Identifies that the ready-flip fires the heavy CI suite per PR into a shared, fixed-concurrency runner pool, so N at once queue and every check pends for minutes, courting pool/runner exhaustion for other lanes
Prescribes staggering the ready-flips to a small in-flight window sized to the runner pool, draining then flipping the next batch, for the same throughput without contention
Distinguishes the ready-flip admission point (runner budget) from the merge-seat / not-red admission rules (the merge action) and from a shared model/API quota (checks pending, not lanes erroring)

evals.prompt: My fix lanes run under a 'minimal patch, stop when the fix is in and tests pass' policy to keep them cheap. One just closed out: it opened a draft PR, the code fix is correct, the fast gates are green -- but it never wrote the changelog fragment or flipped the PR to ready, so the PR is stranded (draft, red on the missing-changelog check). The brief did list 'add changelog fragment, mark ready.' Why did it skip them, and how do I stop it recurring?
evals.expected_output: The lane stopped ON PURPOSE, having met a definition of done that never included the finalize steps: a 'minimal patch / stop when fixed' policy defines completion as code-fix + gates-green and treats the post-fix PROCESS steps (changelog fragment, ready-flip, evidence) as out of scope. A standing process-policy default outweighs one line buried in a task brief, so naming the steps in the brief is necessary but not sufficient -- this is a REQUIRED step dropped (the mirror of a brief prohibition being a soft control). Fix: fold the process steps INTO the lane's acceptance / Done-when (SKILL.md Work-item contract), so 'fixed' is not 'done' until the changelog fragment and ready-flip are in -- change what done MEANS for the lane, do not just repeat the steps; OR make the process tail the ORCHESTRATOR's explicitly-owned job (the small mechanical finalize), assigned to one owner. One of the two must own the tail; the failure is when neither does. Read a draft red only on a missing changelog fragment as stranded-by-contract (the fix is sound, the tail was truncated), not a code defect to re-review. Distinct from 'land the fix, then finalize separately': there the finalize was ATTEMPTED and orphaned by a process/retry loop burning the turn (fix: decouple + idempotent + bound); here it was NEVER in the definition of done (fix: widen the acceptance contract). (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Identifies the root cause as a 'minimal patch / stop when fixed' contract truncating the lane's definition of done to code-fix + gates-green, so the required post-fix process steps are skipped deliberately
Notes the brief alone is insufficient -- a standing process-policy default outweighs one brief line (a required step dropped, the mirror of a brief prohibition as a soft control)

Prescribes folding the process steps into the lane's acceptance / Done-when (SKILL.md Work-item contract) so 'fixed' is not 'done', OR making the tail the orchestrator's explicitly-owned job -- exactly one owner
Distinguishes this (finalize never in the definition of done) from 'land the fix, then finalize separately' (finalize attempted but orphaned by a process/retry loop)

evals.prompt: A stranded PR (draft, red only on a missing changelog fragment; its lane stopped and its worktree was reaped) needs finishing. My redispatched producer lane is resuming it to add the fragment and flip it ready, and at the same time my merge-seat holder found it blocking the drain and is unstranding it to merge. Both are just finishing the same small tail, so it's fine for both to proceed, right?
evals.expected_output: No -- a stranded PR has NO live owner, and an orphan with no owner attracts two recoverers: the producer (resumed to finish its lane) and the merge-seat holder (unstranding to clear its queue). Both write the SAME branch to complete the SAME tail seconds apart -- a dual PUSH to one ref: a non-fast-forward for the loser, a force-push clobber if either overrides, or two divergent finish commits (one adding the fragment, one flipping ready) that collide. It is not dual WORK on disjoint files (the ownership-map / occupancy check reads empty because the lane is dead) -- it is dual WRITE to one branch, which one-writer-per-branch forbids, arising because the branch's writer stopped and nothing re-established a single owner. Fixes: (1) treat recovering/unstranding a stranded PR as an EXCLUSIVE step -- claim it before acting (the exclusive_role field of the claim registry, applied to unstranding, not only the merge seat) and refuse to recover a PR another owner is already unstranding; (2) assign unstranding to ONE role by default -- the merge-seat holder is natural (already serialized, already touches the branch to merge), so fold 'finish the tail, then merge' into the seat and have the resumed producer stand down on any PR the seat is unstranding (either owner works; the invariant is exactly one); (3) verify the in-flight write actually landed on the remote before concluding recovery, never the recoverer's own 'pushed' claim. Distinct from what STRANDS the PR (a truncated lane contract) and from the ownership-map dual-write rule (which stops a duplicate lane on a LIVE objective via occupancy -- here the lane is dead, so the race is between two recoverers, resolved by a recovery claim). (verification-handback.md.)
expectations: Rejects letting both proceed; identifies a stranded PR as having no live owner, so producer and merge-seat holder both recover it -- a dual WRITE (non-fast-forward / force-push / divergent finish commits) to one branch, not dual work on disjoint files

Requires treating recovery/unstranding as an exclusive step claimed before acting (exclusive_role in the claim registry applied to unstranding), refusing to recover a PR another owner is already unstranding
Assigns unstranding to exactly one owner by default (the merge-seat holder is natural), with the other party standing down -- the invariant is exactly one owner, not which one

Verifies the in-flight write landed on the remote before concluding recovery; distinguishes this recovery-ownership race from the ownership-map dual-write rule (occupancy reads empty because the lane is dead) and from what stranded the PR

evals.prompt: Two of my peer sessions coordinate through a shared tracker thread. Each posts 'taking X' before starting an item to avoid collisions. They still shipped two PRs for the same item X -- each posted 'taking X' within a second of the other, before reading the other's post. My fix is to make each peer re-read the thread more carefully right before posting. Will that close it?
evals.expected_output: No -- re-reading harder cannot close a simultaneity window; the claim MECHANISM is the defect. A comment on an append-only thread is an append, not a compare-and-swap: every post succeeds, so 'taking X' never FAILS and never tells the poster someone already took X -- the channel is eventually-consistent, never a mutex, and it happily stores both claims. The fix is a claim TOKEN whose namespace is the item and whose creation is ATOMIC on that namespace, so the second creator's attempt fails rather than appends: an exclusive file create (O_CREAT|O_EXCL / a lock file that errors if it exists), an atomic rename into a per-item path, or a deterministically-named branch/ref (claim/<item-id>) whose second push of that same new ref the forge rejects -- the failed create IS the collision signal, delivered at claim time to the loser. A comment or a registry ROW is fine to RECORD and read a claim but not to WIN one (appending a registry row has the same non-atomicity: two rows land, neither create failed) -- keep the structured registry as the readable record, write the row AFTER winning the token. Fall back to post-hoc arbitration (claim-first + earliest-UTC-wins, #933) only where no atomic primitive exists (a plain thread, last-write-wins assignment); it is strictly weaker -- both must post, both re-read, the loser stands down, and the window remains. Distinct from #933 (corrective: arbitrate the dup after it happens) -- this is preventive (the second claim fails, so no dup starts); from #834 domain partition (removes the shared item; this keeps it shared and makes claiming it atomic); and from 'commit a structured registry' (claim SHAPE vs claim ATOMICITY -- a perfectly structured row still loses the race if it is an append). (multi-session-coordination.md.)
expectations: Rejects 're-read more carefully' -- a comment/announcement on an append-only thread is not atomic (every post succeeds), so it cannot arbitrate two simultaneous claims and re-reading cannot close the window

Prescribes a claim token whose creation is atomic on the item's namespace so the second create FAILS (O_CREAT|O_EXCL lock file, atomic rename, or a deterministically-named branch/ref whose second push is rejected) -- the failed create is the claim-time collision signal

Keeps a structured registry/comment as the readable RECORD but not the thing that WINS the claim; writes the row after winning the token; falls back to post-hoc arbitration only where no atomic primitive exists
Distinguishes the preventive atomic token from post-hoc corrective arbitration and from domain partition (removing the shared item)

evals.prompt: Four of my coding agents share one build box, and each runs the full local test suite before it pushes. One lane's headless-browser render test just timed out, so its pre-push gate went red. That lane opened a bug and started patching the render path as a regression. The other three lanes were mid-build at the moment it failed. Is treating this red as a code regression right -- and if not, what should the lane do before it touches the render path?
evals.expected_output: No -- do not conclude a regression from that red, and do not bypass the gate either; both are wrong on a FIRST red under aggregate load. Four full local test suites on one shared box can exhaust its CPU / RAM / file descriptors, so a headless-browser render times out (or a timing assertion trips, or a suite flakes) in a way that is indistinguishable, from inside one lane, from a real regression the diff introduced -- and three siblings were mid-build, which is exactly the contention window. A failure that appears only under fan-out concurrency is contention, not a defect, until reproduced at LOW concurrency (parallel-audit.md section 0). So before patching anything: QUIESCE the box -- pause or kill the other heavy lanes (shed the test runner's own browsers, keep the app's dev server) -- then re-run the SPECIFIC failing check on the IDENTICAL commit. A pass on the quiesced box proves the red was contention (no bug, no fix cycle); only a failure that STILL reproduces at low concurrency is a candidate regression that enters the fix queue. Crucially, a same-commit rerun taken WITHOUT quiescing is not a valid disambiguation -- under sustained contention it keeps failing and would wrongly flip the verdict to 'regression,' the exact wasted cycle this avoids. Prevent it up front by throttling heavy gate lanes on MEASURED load (free RAM + the swap trend; the peer-aggregate form is a shared machine-wide heavy-lane reservation) and running locally only the gate CI actually enforces, so fewer contention-flakes reach the verdict step at all. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Rejects concluding a regression AND rejects bypassing the gate on the first red -- several full local gates on one shared box produce contention timeouts/flakes indistinguishable from a real defect from inside one lane

Prescribes re-running the specific failing check IN ISOLATION on a quiesced box (pause/kill the other heavy lanes, shedding test browsers not the dev server) on the identical commit; a pass-alone proves contention, only a failure that still reproduces at low concurrency is a candidate regression

Names the trap that a same-commit rerun WITHOUT quiescing is not a valid disambiguation -- it keeps failing under sustained contention and wrongly flips the verdict to regression, the wasted fix cycle the load-flaky bounded-rerun assumes is already ruled out

Adds the prevention side: throttle heavy lanes on measured load (free RAM + swap trend / shared heavy-lane reservation) and run locally only the gate CI enforces, so fewer contention-flakes reach the verdict

evals.prompt: Our auto-merge bot runs under its own dedicated GitHub account, separate from the humans on the repo (humans open PRs too). To keep it from merging a human's in-progress PR, we maintain a checked-in do-not-merge.txt that lists the human PR numbers and branches it must skip; the bot merges anything green that is not on that list. It has worked for weeks. Is this a sound way to keep the bot off human PRs, or is there a failure mode?
evals.expected_output: There is a real failure mode, and it is the exclusion list itself. Because the bot has its OWN account, the reliable ownership signal is already the author field -- so scope the auto-merger to PRs whose author POSITIVELY matches the bot's own account and default-deny every other PR; a human's PR is then out of scope BY CONSTRUCTION, not by having been remembered. A hand-maintained do-not-merge list inverts that: it is a denylist only as current as its last edit, and the PR it never learned about is the NEXT human PR -- so the first time a human opens a PR nobody has added yet, the bot sees it is green and not on the list and auto-merges the human's mid-review work. 'Worked for weeks' is survivorship, not safety; it holds only until an unlisted human PR appears. Fix: filter by the author-identity match (default-deny anything not positively confirmed the bot's own), and verify the match against the PR's real author rather than an assumed token identity (a green-looking identity is a floor, not proof). The hand-maintained list is the right tool only in the OPPOSITE case -- shared identity, where agents authenticate as the human and there is no author signal to key on, so you must manufacture an ownership mark (label / branch-prefix / allowlist) with default-deny. Here a distinct identity exists, so the author match strictly dominates the list. (merge-queue-worktrees.md.)
expectations: Identifies the failure mode as the hand-maintained exclusion (denylist) itself: it goes stale, and the next human PR it never learned about is auto-merged mid-review the moment it is green

Prescribes filtering by the author-identity match against the bot's OWN account with default-deny, so a human PR is out of scope by construction rather than by being listed; rejects 'worked for weeks' as survivorship not safety
Requires verifying the match against the PR's real author, not an assumed token identity (a green-looking identity is a floor, not proof)

Gives the discriminator: a manufactured mark / list is correct only in the SHARED-identity case (no author signal to key on); where a distinct identity exists the author-identity match strictly dominates a hand-maintained list

evals.prompt: One of my agents runs under a standing rule: every work cycle it posts a short status update to a shared board so a sibling agent can follow its progress. The sibling has posted nothing, replied to nothing, and left no acknowledgement for eight cycles straight -- about twelve days -- and my agent has dutifully posted its status on the board every one of those cycles because its rule just says 'post status each cycle.' Is that the right thing to keep doing, and if not, what should it do instead -- and how should it tell an ordinary temporary quiet spell apart from a sibling that is actually gone?
evals.expected_output: No. A shared board the sibling never reads is not coordination; posting to it on a fixed timer every cycle spends cycles for no benefit and adds noise, and the 'post status each cycle' rule was written with no check that a reader still exists. But the agent must not overcorrect on a single quiet cycle either: one or two cycles with no response is an ordinary temporary gap, not proof the sibling is gone. The discriminator is a run of CONSECUTIVE cycles with no response of any kind attributable to the sibling itself -- no reply, ack, or new entry of its own -- at or beyond a pre-set count; below that count, keep posting, and only a sustained run at or past it counts as the sibling genuinely being gone. Once that point is reached, stop (or sharply cut the frequency of) the every-cycle posting instead of continuing on the timer, and raise the sibling's prolonged absence once to the owner or another channel that is actually read, rather than posting the same update into the unread board again next cycle. The correct behaviour sits between two failures: posting forever on the timer, and hard-stopping the instant the sibling misses one cycle.
expectations: Rejects continuing to post every cycle on the fixed timer to a board the sibling is not reading -- a one-directional channel with no reader is not coordination, only spent cycles and noise, and the 'post each cycle' rule never re-checks that a reader exists

Requires a sustained run of CONSECUTIVE non-responses at or past a pre-set count before concluding the sibling is gone; a single quiet cycle is an ordinary temporary gap, so hard-stopping on the first missed cycle is as wrong as never stopping
On a confirmed run, stops or sharply reduces the timed posting rather than continuing to fire on the timer
Raises the sibling's prolonged absence to the owner or a channel that is actually read, once -- not another post into the unread board each cycle

evals.prompt: Fifteen build lanes ran overnight against a backlog. Every lane pushed a green branch and every gate passed -- solid delivery. Each lane's final handback report, though, opens by restating its brief in full, walks through every debugging step it tried before the one that worked, includes a worked example of the fix applied to a second file 'for illustration,' and only then states the verdict, branch, and gate status in its last two lines. Nothing in the reports is false and nothing required is missing. Is there still something worth fixing here, and if so what's the actual problem and the fix?
evals.expected_output: Yes -- the reports themselves are a cost problem even though nothing in them is false or missing. Every lane's narration and worked-example padding is tokens that lane is billed to generate, and wherever the handback reaches an orchestrator's own context it is tokens the orchestrator re-pays to read -- cost scales roughly as lane count times output length per lane times rounds, so fifteen lanes each padding by a few paragraphs is a large, avoidable multiply, not a per-lane rounding error. This is a distinct axis from 'report the artifact, not the activity' (that rule is about a status being truthful -- artifact vs transcript -- not about how many words carry an otherwise-truthful report) and from baking a terse register into the agent definition (that is the enforcement mechanism; this is what the terse register should be terse ABOUT). The fix is not to drop required content -- the verdict, file:line, branch/SHA, and each gate's pass/fail already at the bottom are exactly the required Output-contract fields and must stay. The fix is to cut everything ahead of them: the restated brief, the blow-by-blow of steps that did not work, and the illustrative worked example nobody asked for. Size the closing handback to what the next decision consumes, not to the transcript that produced it. (fanout-host-sizing.md.)
expectations: Identifies the reports' own verbosity/padding as a real problem despite every gate passing and nothing false or missing -- distinct from a delivery defect
States the cost mechanism as lane count x output-length-per-lane x rounds, so per-lane padding compounds across many lanes and rounds

Distinguishes this from 'report the artifact, not the activity' (truthfulness of status content) and from baking a terse register into the agent definition (the enforcement mechanism) -- this is what that terse register should be terse about

Prescribes cutting narration/restated-brief/unrequested worked example while keeping every required Output-contract field (verdict, file:line, branch/SHA, gate pass/fail) intact -- terse the prose, not the fields

evals.prompt: A lane's PR touches a page-rendering component. The gate requires either narrow/wide screenshots or a standalone 'No UX change: <reason>' line in the PR body. The lane's body reads: 'This PR only swaps a retry constant from 3 to 5; no UX change results from this edit, and tests are green.' The gate runs and reports the UX-evidence requirement as unmet, so CI reds a diff whose author is confident is UX-neutral. Did the lane do something wrong, and what should it do differently?
